entries.title: Access Controls
entries.productionQuestion: An auditor asks who can read production data. Can you answer in minutes?
entries.learningDelta: Access control evidence requires identity, role, approval, and review; shared accounts and standing admin rights break the story
objectives: Answer an access question from a system of record instead of reconstructing it from screenshots.
Distinguish least privilege, separation of duties, and review evidence.
Find the access patterns that make attribution impossible.
Design a review cycle that produces current evidence without slowing delivery.

entries.title: Action Items That Land
entries.productionQuestion: The last postmortem had 20 action items and none shipped. What do you change?
entries.learningDelta: Action items need an owner, due date, verification, and prioritization; unowned items are wishes
objectives: Write an action item that names an owner, a due date, and a verification.
Prioritize prevention work against limited engineering capacity.
Explain why a long, unprioritized action list produces recurrence.
Track completion with evidence rather than a status field.

entries.title: Adding Readers During an Incident
entries.productionQuestion: The primary is overloaded, so you add a secondary. Why did latency get worse?
entries.learningDelta: A new secondary performs an initial sync and then serves cold reads; it increases primary load and replication pressure before it helps
objectives: Trace how initial sync adds load to the primary and the replication path.
Explain why a new secondary cannot reduce read pressure until sync completes and its cache warms.
Choose between a secondary sync source, waiting for off-peak traffic, and routing reads.
Decide when adding a reader is the wrong response to a write-bound primary.

entries.title: Admission Control: Bounded Queues and Priorities
entries.productionQuestion: The queue is 30 seconds deep and clients time out before service; what should the server do?
entries.learningDelta: Admission control keeps queues bounded and rejects or prioritizes work before latency becomes useless
objectives: Explain why an unbounded queue converts a load spike into a long outage.
Choose a queue bound from the deadline rather than from memory.
Design a priority and reservation policy that protects critical work.
Distinguish total rejection from rejection of the critical class.

entries.title: Aggregation Pipeline Performance
entries.productionQuestion: An aggregation pipeline is slow even with an index. Where is the work happening?
entries.learningDelta: Pipeline stage order determines whether indexes, memory, and disk are used; early filters and limits reduce work
objectives: Trace how many documents enter each stage of an aggregation pipeline.
Explain why a $match after a blocking stage cannot use an index.
Recognize the 100 MB per-stage memory limit and the effect of allowDiskUse.
Reorder a pipeline so filters and limits reduce the work done by blocking stages.

entries.title: ALB Connection Limit Reached: Sharding to NLB
entries.productionQuestion: Your ALB is healthy, targets are healthy, and you raised the capacity ceiling. New connections are still dropped at peak. What now?
entries.learningDelta: ALB scale limits are per load balancer and per node; at scale you shard across ALBs behind an NLB, not just raise a single ceiling
objectives: Locate a per-ALB connection bottleneck using rejected connections, node count, and LCU.
Explain why raising an illustrative per-ALB ceiling cannot exceed the 100-node limit.
Compare DNS-weighted ALB sharding with an NLB front door by cost, routing, and failure mode.
Design a sharded path that keeps targets healthy and clients connected.

entries.title: ALB LCU: Capacity and Cost Together
entries.productionQuestion: The bill doubled after a traffic change and the ALB is near its LCU limit. Which dimension moved?
entries.learningDelta: LCU bills the highest of new connections, active connections, processed bytes, and rule evaluations; the same traffic can be limited by different dimensions
objectives: Attribute an ALB bill to the LCU dimension that actually sets it.
Predict how response size, connection lifetime, reuse, and rule count move cost.
Distinguish an LCU cost overrun from an availability incident.
Reduce LCU demand without moving the bottleneck to targets or clients.

entries.title: ALB Rule Priority and Order
entries.productionQuestion: A new host rule works in staging but not production. What wins?
entries.learningDelta: ALB listener rules evaluate in priority order; the first match wins, so broad rules can shadow specific ones
objectives: Trace a request through listener rules in priority order.
Explain why a more specific condition does not automatically win.
Diagnose a shadowed rule from target group traffic and access logs.
Design a rule order that keeps specific routes ahead of broad fallbacks.

entries.title: ALB Target Groups: Registration and Health
entries.productionQuestion: The ALB returns 503 while the tasks are running and healthy. What do you check?
entries.learningDelta: An ALB only routes to healthy registered targets; health check path, port, and security groups decide registration
objectives: Distinguish a running task from a registered, healthy target.
Explain which conditions produce an ALB 503 and which produce a target error.
Read target health reason codes and map them to path, port, or security group causes.
Fix registration before tuning capacity or health-check timing.

entries.title: ALB Target Registration for ECS
entries.productionQuestion: A task is running but receives no traffic. What registration state do you check?
entries.learningDelta: ECS registers tasks by IP or instance; target group health, security groups, and ports decide traffic
objectives: Trace a task from RUNNING to healthy target through registration, health check, port, and security group.
Explain why an awsvpc task needs IP targets and what fails with instance targets.
Separate a registration failure from a target health check failure using target health state and reason codes.

entries.title: Alert Fatigue: Measure Actionability
entries.productionQuestion: The team gets 60 pages a week and ignores half. Which alerts should exist?
entries.learningDelta: Alert quality is measured by actionable pages per incident; every noisy page trains responders to ignore the next one
objectives: Separate page volume from the number of actionable pages.
Measure missed incidents alongside pager load instead of optimizing one number.
Explain how rule count, thresholds, deduplication, and ownership change the queue.
Choose which alerts should page, which should ticket, and who owns each.

entries.title: Anomaly Detection Pitfalls
entries.productionQuestion: The detector pages every Monday at 9 a.m. and no one is surprised. What is wrong?
entries.learningDelta: Statistical anomalies are not incidents; seasonality, trends, and missing data create false positives that need guardrails
objectives: Explain why a baseline shorter than the seasonal period misreads a normal peak.
Separate detector sensitivity from the definition of an incident.
Recognize how missing data changes the anomaly score and the page.
Add coverage and seasonality guardrails without hiding real failures.

entries.title: Anycast: Same IP, Many Places
entries.productionQuestion: Users worldwide hit one IP but land in different regions. How does that work, and what breaks?
entries.learningDelta: Anycast advertises the same prefix from many sites; BGP chooses a path, so routing changes can shift traffic and create asymmetric failures
objectives: Explain how the same anycast address can be served from multiple locations without a global load balancer.
Predict how a BGP path change redistributes traffic across points of presence.
Diagnose an overloaded PoP after a routing change and choose a capacity or steering response.
Distinguish ingress concentration from return-path asymmetry.

entries.title: APM Sampling: See the Errors That Matter
entries.productionQuestion: Trace sampling is 1% and a 0.2% error class is invisible. How do you sample?
entries.learningDelta: Uniform head sampling is cheap but blind to rare errors; retention and error-biased sampling preserve the traces you need
objectives: Distinguish head sampling from error-biased or tail sampling by what they can see.
Compute the retained volume and rare-error visibility of a sampling plan.
Explain why a low uniform sample rate can hide a rare error class.
Choose a sampling and retention design that fits a trace budget.

entries.title: Artifact Promotion
entries.productionQuestion: A release is approved in staging; what exactly moves to production?
entries.learningDelta: Promotion moves the same immutable artifact and provenance, with environment config applied separately
objectives: Describe what a promotion record must contain to be auditable.
Explain why rebuilding during promotion loses the staged result.
Keep environment configuration outside the promoted artifact.
Verify the promoted digest at production admission.

entries.title: Audit Logs
entries.productionQuestion: An audit trail is missing the actor for a privileged change. What fields are required?
entries.learningDelta: Audit logs need actor, action, target, time, outcome, and source, with integrity and retention; they must exclude secrets
objectives: Specify the fields that make a privileged action attributable.
Separate an audit record from an application debug log.
Protect the audit trail with integrity, retention, and least privilege.
Investigate a privileged change from the actor through the recorded outcome.

entries.title: Audit Trails
entries.productionQuestion: An auditor asks for the change history of a production role. Can you reconstruct it?
entries.learningDelta: Audit trails combine control-plane logs, approvals, and change records with synchronized time and integrity
objectives: Reconstruct a privileged change across the control plane, approval system, and change record.
Identify which fields make an event attributable and which make it orderable.
Evaluate timestamp synchronization and log integrity as evidence properties.
Explain why an archived log is not a defensible trail without scope and retention.

entries.title: Aurora Backtrack
entries.productionQuestion: A bad migration changed data 20 minutes ago. Can you rewind instead of restoring?
entries.learningDelta: Aurora Backtrack rewinds cluster state within a retention window, but it is not a substitute for backups and has limits
objectives: Compare backtrack, point-in-time recovery, and restore by RTO and scope.
Explain the retention window and target-time constraints.
Quantify the writes lost when rewinding to before a bad change.
Decide when backtrack is unsafe or insufficient.

entries.title: Aurora Global Database
entries.productionQuestion: You need a secondary region for disaster recovery and local reads. What does Aurora Global Database replicate?
entries.learningDelta: Aurora Global Database replicates storage asynchronously to secondary regions; read replicas serve local reads and promotion changes the writer
objectives: Explain what Aurora Global Database replicates and what stays regional.
Separate storage replication lag from the recovery point objective exposed by promotion.
Place local reads in a secondary Region and predict their freshness.
Describe what promotion changes for writers, readers, endpoints, and other secondary clusters.

entries.title: Aurora Serverless Scaling
entries.productionQuestion: A serverless database is slow after idle periods. What is happening?
entries.learningDelta: Aurora Serverless scales capacity in units and may need to resume; pooling, min capacity, and warm traffic change the experience
objectives: Explain Aurora capacity units and the difference between a resumed and a warm cluster.
Relate minimum capacity and pool warmth to cold-start latency.
Predict when scale-up lags a traffic ramp.
Choose a capacity floor from the latency SLO and the idle pattern.

entries.title: Aurora Write Forwarding
entries.productionQuestion: A secondary-region app needs writes but must not send them to a stale local writer. What does write forwarding do?
entries.learningDelta: Write forwarding sends writes from a secondary cluster to the primary writer, adding latency and preserving a single writer
objectives: Trace a forwarded write from the secondary-region client through the primary writer and back.
Explain why write forwarding adds latency but does not create a second writer.
Predict when a forwarded write can time out after the primary has already committed it.
Choose between forwarding, a direct primary connection, and a session consistency mode.

entries.title: Automated Rollback
entries.productionQuestion: A release raises 5xx at 3 a.m. How fast can rollback happen without a human?
entries.learningDelta: Automated rollback uses health and metric gates plus a tested rollback path; the recovery time is bounded by detection and artifact availability
objectives: Break recovery time into detection, decision, and rollback execution.
Explain how a metric gate triggers an automated rollback without a human.
Identify the artifact and schema conditions that make rollback possible.
Choose detection sensitivity that limits exposure without causing rollback loops.

entries.title: Autoscaling Policy Design
entries.productionQuestion: A service scales on CPU but the bottleneck is queue depth. What policy do you use?
entries.learningDelta: Scaling policies must follow the actual bottleneck metric and account for startup, cooldowns, and capacity limits
objectives: Match a scaling policy to the metric that actually limits throughput.
Read desired capacity, in-service capacity, and startup lag as separate signals.
Diagnose a policy that scales on a misleading resource metric.
Choose a target, startup allowance, and capacity ceiling that survive a ramp.

entries.title: Backpressure in Streaming
entries.productionQuestion: The producer outruns consumers and lag grows without bound. Where do you apply backpressure?
entries.learningDelta: Backpressure can throttle producers, buffer durably in the log, or shed work; the log is not infinite and lag is a debt
objectives: Explain why a durable log delays backpressure instead of removing it.
Estimate buffer fill time from produce rate, consumer capacity, and buffer size.
Compare throttling, scaling consumers, and shedding work by what each one protects.
Choose a backpressure point that keeps accepted throughput and downstream state correct.

entries.title: Backpressure: Make the Producer Slow Down
entries.productionQuestion: The consumer is slower than the producer and the queue is growing; where does backpressure belong?
entries.learningDelta: Backpressure propagates capacity signals upstream; bounded queues and producer throttling prevent unbounded memory and latency
objectives: Explain how an unbounded queue turns a throughput mismatch into a memory failure.
Choose where the capacity signal should act: producer, queue, or consumer.
Compare dropping, blocking, and throttling by what they protect and what they cost.
Design a bounded buffer whose overflow behavior the product can explain.

entries.title: Backup and Restore
entries.productionQuestion: A restore of one shard completes but the cluster is inconsistent. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Cluster-consistent backups require coordination across shards and config servers; restoring one node is not a cluster restore
objectives: Identify the unit of a sharded-cluster backup: shards, config servers, and one cluster time.
Explain why restoring one shard or omitting config metadata leaves a cluster inconsistent.
Choose between a coordinated snapshot and a logical dump for a given recovery objective.
Plan a restore verification that checks routing metadata and cross-shard documents, not just row counts.

entries.title: Backups and Point-in-Time Recovery
entries.productionQuestion: A bad migration deletes rows at 14:07. How do you restore without losing 14:00–14:07?
entries.learningDelta: PITR combines a base backup with continuous logs; recovery point and restore time are different objectives
objectives: Explain how a base backup plus archived write-ahead log defines a recoverable window.
Choose a recovery target second and distinguish it from the time the restore finishes.
Calculate the data-loss window when the target is outside retention or its log is not archived yet.
Design and test a restore that reports achieved RPO and RTO rather than configured values.

entries.title: Batch vs Service
entries.productionQuestion: A nightly job runs as a service and restarts forever. What should it be?
entries.learningDelta: Services maintain desired count; batch jobs run to completion and retry differently, with different observability
objectives: Match a workload to an ECS service, a standalone scheduled task, or an AWS Batch job.
Explain why a service restarts a finite job after a successful exit.
Design retries and completion signals for a nightly job without duplicate side effects.

entries.title: BGP for Hybrid Networking
entries.productionQuestion: Two paths advertise the same prefix and traffic takes the slower one. Why?
entries.learningDelta: BGP selects paths by attributes such as local preference, AS path, and MED; failover depends on what changes
objectives: Apply the BGP best-path order to two competing paths with the same prefix.
Explain why a higher local preference beats a shorter AS path and why MED is a weaker signal.
Distinguish a control-plane failure from a data-plane failure that leaves BGP established.
Design a failover test that proves the backup becomes selected, not just reachable.

entries.title: Big Keys: One Key, Many Problems
entries.productionQuestion: Redis latency spikes every time a 50MB key is read. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Big keys consume bandwidth, block the single-threaded event loop during operations, and create uneven shard memory
objectives: Explain why one large value delays every command on its shard, not only the read that fetched it.
Separate event-loop blocking from bandwidth cost and from memory imbalance.
Find a big key with SCAN-based sampling, MEMORY USAGE, and per-shard latency instead of a cluster average.
Split or remove a big key without assuming that splitting alone reduces the bytes a read must return.

entries.title: Blameless Postmortems
entries.productionQuestion: The postmortem names the engineer who ran the command and no one shares details. What is wrong?
entries.learningDelta: Blameless analysis focuses on conditions and system design; blame suppresses the information needed to prevent recurrence
objectives: Explain what blameless analysis changes and what it does not excuse.
Rewrite an individual-focused statement as a set of contributing conditions.
Recognize how blame reduces the information available to the review.
Distinguish a contributing factor from a root cause and from an action item.

entries.title: Blue-Green Database Migrations
entries.productionQuestion: Both blue and green must run during cutover. How do you migrate the database?
entries.learningDelta: Blue-green schema changes require expand/contract compatibility so both versions can read and write during the transition
objectives: Explain why a blue-green cutover still leaves two code versions sharing one database.
Sequence schema changes so both versions can read and write during the transition.
Identify the point where a destructive change blocks rollback.
Use dual writes and backfill coverage to protect old and new readers.

entries.title: Blue-Green Deployments
entries.productionQuestion: A blue-green deploy is ready but the database migration is not reversible. Do you cut over?
entries.learningDelta: Blue-green gives fast traffic cutover and rollback, but shared state and schema changes can make the old environment unusable
objectives: Explain how traffic cutover and rollback work in a blue-green deployment.
Separate environment readiness from shared database compatibility.
Recognize when a destructive schema change breaks the rollback path.
Choose an expand/contract sequence that keeps both versions compatible.

entries.title: Build Once, Deploy Many
entries.productionQuestion: A config change requires a rebuild and staging diverges. How do you deploy the same artifact with different config?
entries.learningDelta: Configuration belongs outside the artifact; environment-specific config is injected at deploy time, with validation
objectives: Separate the immutable artifact from environment-specific configuration.
Explain why baking configuration into an image forces a rebuild per environment.
Predict which configuration differences produce production-only failures.
Design deploy-time configuration validation that fails before traffic arrives.

entries.title: Bulkheads: Isolate the Blast Radius
entries.productionQuestion: One tenant's batch job is starving interactive traffic; how do you isolate it?
entries.learningDelta: Pools, queues, and concurrency limits per workload contain saturation to one bulkhead
objectives: Explain how a shared worker pool turns one workload's backlog into another workload's latency.
Compare shared and isolated pools by interactive SLO and aggregate utilization.
Choose a reservation size and defend the idle capacity it creates.
Recognize when isolation moves the bottleneck instead of removing it.

entries.title: Business Associate Agreements
entries.productionQuestion: You want to use a new observability vendor for a HIPAA workload. What must exist first?
entries.learningDelta: A BAA binds a vendor that handles PHI; without it, the vendor relationship is not compliant regardless of encryption
objectives: Decide when a vendor that touches a health-data workload is a business associate.
Explain what a BAA does and does not prove about a vendor's security.
Place a BAA gate in the data path instead of in a spreadsheet.
Evaluate a vendor onboarding flow for PHI egress and subcontractor risk.

entries.title: Cache Coherence Across Instances
entries.productionQuestion: An update reaches one instance and others serve stale data for minutes. How do you invalidate?
entries.learningDelta: Coherence requires invalidation or versioning across every cache layer; pub/sub is fast but lossy, so TTLs remain a backstop
objectives: Tell a delivery failure from a cache that never received an invalidation.
Compare pub/sub, durable delivery, versioned keys, and TTL backstops by failure mode.
Explain why a lossy invalidation path can look healthy at the broker and stale at the product.
Design a coherence path whose stale window is bounded and observable.

entries.title: Cache Failure
entries.productionQuestion: Redis is down and the database immediately saturates. What is the incident plan?
entries.learningDelta: Cache failure shifts load to the origin; load shedding, negative caching, and a staged recovery prevent a second outage
objectives: Quantify the origin load created by losing a given cache hit rate.
Protect the origin with shedding and stale or negative responses before restoring the cache.
Explain why an immediate full cache restart can cause a second outage.
Sequence cache recovery so the origin and the cache warm up together.

entries.title: Cache Invalidation: Coherence Without Guessing
entries.productionQuestion: An update lands on one instance and other instances serve stale data for minutes; how do you invalidate?
entries.learningDelta: Invalidation is a distributed coherence problem; pub/sub, versioned keys, and short TTLs trade freshness for complexity
objectives: Explain why a local cache and a shared cache have different coherence paths.
Compare TTL expiry, pub/sub invalidation, and versioned keys on freshness and complexity.
Diagnose a stale read from the write, invalidation, and delivery path.
Design a fallback for a missed invalidation message.

entries.title: Cache Penetration: Requests for Missing Keys
entries.productionQuestion: Random IDs miss the cache and hit the database every time. What do you add?
entries.learningDelta: Penetration is repeated lookup of absent keys; negative caching and Bloom filters reject impossible keys early
objectives: Separate cache penetration from a stampede and from an ordinary low hit rate.
Explain what a negative cache stores and why its TTL is a correctness decision.
Read a Bloom filter's false-positive rate from its bits per key.
Choose a filter placement that stops absent-key traffic before the database.

entries.title: Cache Stampede: When TTL Expires at the Wrong Time
entries.productionQuestion: A popular key expires and the database CPU goes to 100%. How do you stop the herd?
entries.learningDelta: A stampede occurs when many concurrent misses recompute one value; single-flight, jitter, and early refresh collapse the work
objectives: Tell a stampede from a capacity problem by aligning database load with cache expiry.
Compare single-flight, TTL jitter, and early refresh by what they collapse and what they cost.
Explain why a high cache hit rate can coexist with a saturated database.
Choose a mitigation that fits the product's freshness and latency budget.

entries.title: Cache Warming After a Cold Start
entries.productionQuestion: A Redis restart leaves an empty cache and the database is overwhelmed. How do you warm it?
entries.learningDelta: Cold caches shift load to the origin; controlled warming, request coalescing, and rate limits prevent a restart from becoming an outage
objectives: Explain why an empty cache moves read load to the origin.
Choose a warmup rate that fills the hot set without saturating the database.
Combine warming with coalescing so live misses do not multiply the preload.
Sequence recovery: protect the origin, warm in waves, then restore traffic.

entries.title: Cache-Aside vs Write-Through
entries.productionQuestion: Writes must be durable and reads must be fast. Where does the cache sit?
entries.learningDelta: Cache-aside leaves the cache optional and can serve stale data; write-through keeps it fresh but adds write latency and failure coupling
objectives: Trace a read and a write through cache-aside and through write-through.
Explain why cache-aside can serve stale data after a successful database write.
Explain why write-through couples write availability to the cache unless it has a bypass.
Choose a strategy from the durability, freshness, and latency requirements of the data.

entries.title: Caching Strategies: Where the Write Goes
entries.productionQuestion: The product needs fast reads and durable writes; which cache strategy fits?
entries.learningDelta: Cache-aside keeps the cache optional, write-through keeps it fresh at write cost, write-behind risks data loss
objectives: Compare cache-aside, write-through, and write-behind on the write path.
Explain why write-behind can acknowledge a write that the cache then loses.
Choose a strategy from a durability and freshness requirement, not from read latency alone.
Name the failure behavior of each strategy when the cache is unavailable.

entries.title: Canary Capacity Fallacy
entries.productionQuestion: A canary passes at 5% traffic and the service fails at 100%. Why?
entries.learningDelta: A canary at low traffic does not exercise capacity, caches, locks, or downstream limits at full scale
objectives: Explain why error rate and latency at a small traffic share can miss a capacity failure.
Project full-scale resource demand from per-request behavior.
Choose a load test or traffic step that exercises the resource that will break.
Design a gate that fails before full rollout saturates a shared limit.

entries.title: Canary Deployments
entries.productionQuestion: A release has a bug that affects 1% of requests. How does a canary help?
entries.learningDelta: A canary exposes a small traffic slice to the new version and gates promotion on observed signals
objectives: Explain how a canary limits blast radius without proving the release is safe.
Compare per-version error rate with the blended service error rate.
Detect a gate that passes because stable traffic dilutes canary errors.
Decide when the canary slice is large enough to support promotion.

entries.title: Canary Through the Mesh
entries.productionQuestion: The canary has 5% traffic and no errors; can you increase to 100%?
entries.learningDelta: A canary needs a representative metric gate, enough traffic, and capacity headroom; low traffic hides tail failures
objectives: Explain what a mesh-weighted canary proves and what its traffic share leaves untested.
Compute the canary sample size from weight, request rate, and gate window.
Compare canary per-pod density with production density before promoting.
Choose a gate and rollback condition that cover capacity at 100%.

entries.title: Canary with a Metric Gate
entries.productionQuestion: The canary passes error rate but fails at full rollout because of capacity. What gate was missing?
entries.learningDelta: A canary gate must cover error rate, latency, saturation, and capacity at the target scale, with enough traffic for confidence
objectives: Separate error-rate gates from latency, saturation, and capacity gates.
Explain why a canary at low traffic can pass while full rollout saturates a shared dependency.
Choose a canary share and gate window that produce enough samples for the decision.
Design a promotion sequence with a rollback path when a gate fails.

entries.title: CAP and PACELC: The Trade You Cannot Avoid
entries.productionQuestion: The network partition is real; which writes do you accept and which do you refuse?
entries.learningDelta: CAP applies only during partitions; PACELC extends the tradeoff to latency versus consistency in normal operation
objectives: State CAP precisely: consistency, availability, and partition tolerance are not three everyday choices.
Predict read and write outcomes for strong, available, and quorum modes during a partition.
Use PACELC to explain the latency cost of consistency when the network is healthy.
Defend a consistency choice by naming the conflict policy and the user-visible failure.

entries.title: Capacity Headroom and N+1
entries.productionQuestion: You are at 60% peak utilization with three AZs; what happens when one AZ is lost?
entries.learningDelta: N+1 headroom must cover the loss of the largest failure domain at peak, not at average
objectives: Calculate post-failure utilization from pre-failure utilization and zone count.
Distinguish N+1 from N+2 and name when each is justified.
Explain why average utilization overstates available headroom.
Size a fleet from peak demand and the largest failure domain.

entries.title: Capacity Models
entries.productionQuestion: The quarterly forecast is a spreadsheet with no queueing. What is missing?
entries.learningDelta: Capacity models combine arrival rate, service time, concurrency, headroom, and failure domains; averages alone mislead
objectives: Convert peak arrival rate and service time into required concurrency.
Apply a utilization target and a failure-domain reserve to the model.
Compare a provisioned plan with the model requirement.
Defend the assumptions that move the capacity number most.

entries.title: Capacity Providers
entries.productionQuestion: A service moves to a capacity provider and tasks fail to place. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Capacity providers define capacity and strategy; weights, base, and instance types determine placement and cost
objectives: Read a capacity provider strategy and predict which provider receives each task.
Explain why base is a floor and weight is a distribution rule rather than a fallback.
Diagnose tasks that stay unplaced when a secondary provider runs out of capacity.
Choose between Fargate and Auto Scaling group providers with cost and capacity in view.

entries.title: CDN Cache Keys: Hit Rate by Design
entries.productionQuestion: CDN hit rate is 30% and origin is overloaded. What belongs in the cache key?
entries.learningDelta: Cache key selection decides reuse; including irrelevant headers fragments the cache, omitting vary-worthy inputs serves wrong content
objectives: Trace how a CDN computes a cache key and why two identical paths can miss.
Measure how high-cardinality headers, cookies, and query strings multiply cache entries.
Separate a fragmentation problem from a correctness problem using hit rate and wrong-content signals.
Design a key that keeps only response-variant inputs while forwarding the rest to the origin.

entries.title: CDN TTL and Purge
entries.productionQuestion: A deploy needs new assets immediately but long TTLs keep old ones cached. What do you do?
entries.learningDelta: TTL trades freshness for hit rate; purge is fast but operationally risky and may not reach every edge immediately
objectives: Explain how TTL, revalidation, and purge control freshness at the edge.
Measure the origin cost of short TTLs and the stale window of long TTLs.
Compare overwrite, purge, and versioned URLs by freshness, origin load, and blast radius.
Choose a release strategy that makes a deploy visible without a global purge.

entries.title: Certificate Rotation
entries.productionQuestion: Certificates expire at midnight and the mesh starts failing handshakes. What rotation plan?
entries.learningDelta: Certificate rotation needs overlapping validity, trust bundles, and automated reload; short-lived certs reduce risk but require reliable automation
objectives: Explain how leaf certificates, a trust bundle, and SDS fit together in mesh mTLS.
Distinguish a certificate that was renewed from one the proxy actually loaded.
Predict the failure window when trust bundles do not overlap.
Design a rotation plan with alerts before expiry, not after.

entries.title: Change Data Capture
entries.productionQuestion: A downstream index lags by an hour because it polls the database. Can CDC help?
entries.learningDelta: CDC reads the database log and emits ordered changes; snapshotting, schema changes, and tombstones add complexity
objectives: Explain how log-based CDC differs from polling a table.
Predict lag during an initial snapshot and after a schema change.
Handle tombstones and deletes in a downstream projection.
Choose CDC when ordering and freshness justify its operational cost.

entries.title: Change Freezes
entries.productionQuestion: A freeze is active and a critical fix is needed. What is the exception path?
entries.learningDelta: Freezes reduce change risk but concentrate it; exceptions need review, rollback plans, and a clear owner
objectives: Explain what a change freeze controls and what it moves rather than removes.
Predict how freeze length and change volume concentrate risk at the thaw.
Design an exception path with a bounded decision time, rollback plan, and owner.
Recognize when a slow exception path makes bypass rational.

entries.title: Change Management That Helps
entries.productionQuestion: Every change needs five approvals and incidents still happen. What should change review focus on?
entries.learningDelta: Good change management reviews blast radius, reversibility, observability, and ownership; approval count is not risk control
objectives: Separate approval count from risk review coverage.
Score change risk by blast radius, reversibility, observability, and ownership.
Explain how reviewer capacity becomes a queue and delays every change.
Redesign a review process that shortens lead time without hiding high-risk changes.

entries.title: Change Streams
entries.productionQuestion: A downstream service polls MongoDB every second and adds load. Can it subscribe instead?
entries.learningDelta: Change streams expose a resumable oplog cursor; resume tokens and majority read concern determine durability and replay
objectives: Describe how a change stream cursor follows majority-committed changes without polling queries.
Explain the role of the resume token when a consumer reconnects.
Predict what happens when a consumer is down longer than the oplog retains history.
Choose between polling and a change stream for a downstream integration.

entries.title: Chaos Engineering
entries.productionQuestion: A dependency failure takes down the service despite redundancy. How do you find the gap before production?
entries.learningDelta: Chaos experiments test specific hypotheses with a bounded blast radius, stop conditions, and observability
objectives: Write a chaos hypothesis that names the steady state and the expected behavior.
Bound a fault injection by blast radius, duration, and stop condition.
Explain why observability is part of the experiment design, not an afterthought.
Decide when to abort, roll back, and promote a finding into a fix.

entries.title: Chunk Migration
entries.productionQuestion: The balancer starts migrating chunks and p99 rises. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Chunk migration copies data and updates metadata; it consumes I/O and network and can compete with application traffic
objectives: Trace the copy, catch-up, metadata update, and deletion phases of a chunk migration.
Explain how migration rate, chunk size, and shared I/O capacity affect application latency.
Separate migration load from a hot key or a capacity shortfall.
Control migration with rate, windows, and throttling instead of turning the balancer off forever.

entries.title: CI/CD Pipeline Design
entries.productionQuestion: The pipeline takes 90 minutes and teams bypass it. What do you optimize?
entries.learningDelta: Pipeline speed and reliability determine adoption; parallelism, caching, and staged gates reduce lead time without skipping safety
objectives: Break lead time into work, queue, retry, and approval components.
Explain why feedback time drives pipeline adoption and bypass.
Predict the effect of parallelism, caching, and flaky tests on lead time.
Reduce lead time without removing the safety gates that matter.

entries.title: Circuit Breaking: Fail Fast, Recover Slowly
entries.productionQuestion: The dependency is timing out; how do you stop making it worse without manual intervention?
entries.learningDelta: A breaker converts repeated failures into fast local failures and probes recovery with limited traffic
objectives: Trace the closed, open, and half-open states and the signal that moves between them.
Choose a failure threshold and reset timeout that protect the caller without hiding a real outage.
Explain why an open breaker restores latency and caller capacity but not correctness.
Defend the probe budget and the fallback that remains necessary beside the breaker.

entries.title: Cloud Map
entries.productionQuestion: You need private DNS for 40 services. How does Cloud Map work?
entries.learningDelta: Cloud Map maintains namespaces and service instances; health checks and TTLs control resolution and failover
objectives: Describe the namespace, service, and instance hierarchy that Cloud Map maintains.
Explain how a health check changes which instances answer a discovery query.
Diagnose unhealthy instances that remain registered and receive traffic.

entries.title: Cloudflare and Akamai Behavior
entries.productionQuestion: The same cache rule behaves differently on two CDNs. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Edge providers implement cache keys, purge, and rule evaluation differently; portability requires testing the behavior you depend on
objectives: Compare how Cloudflare and Akamai derive cache keys and scope purges.
Explain why rule evaluation order changes what gets cached and what a purge reaches.
Measure hit rate, stale content, purge lag, and origin load for the same intent on two providers.
Port an edge configuration by translating key fields, purge scope, and rule order, then verifying behavior.

entries.title: Cold Read Replicas
entries.productionQuestion: You add a read replica during an incident and it makes latency worse. Why?
entries.learningDelta: A new replica must catch up and warm its cache; reads routed too early hit cold storage and increase lag
objectives: Explain what a new replica must do before it serves reads safely.
Relate cache warmth and replay progress to read latency.
Sequence read routing after catch-up and warmup.
Predict when adding a replica makes an incident worse.

entries.title: Cold Secondaries
entries.productionQuestion: A secondary has low CPU but serves reads slowly. Why?
entries.learningDelta: A new secondary has a cold WiredTiger cache; serving reads before it warms up increases disk I/O and latency
objectives: Explain why a newly started secondary can have idle CPU and slow reads at the same time.
Relate WiredTiger cache size, working-set coverage, and disk read latency.
Separate a cold-cache latency problem from replication lag or CPU saturation.
Sequence read routing so a new member warms before it takes production traffic.

entries.title: Committed Use
entries.productionQuestion: A three-year commitment saves 40% but the workload may change. How do you decide?
entries.learningDelta: Commitments trade flexibility for discount; forecast confidence, term, and coverage determine the break-even
objectives: Compute the break-even between a commitment discount and unused committed spend.
Separate coverage from utilization when judging a commitment.
Diagnose a commitment that outlives the workload it was bought for.
Choose a term and coverage level from forecast confidence, not from the discount alone.

entries.title: Communication Cadence
entries.productionQuestion: The incident channel is silent for 40 minutes and support invents updates. What cadence?
entries.learningDelta: Regular updates at a fixed cadence reduce uncertainty; internal and external audiences need different detail
objectives: Explain why an update cadence is a commitment, not a best effort.
Separate internal incident detail from customer-facing impact and workaround.
Recognize the cost of both silence and over-communication.
Write an update that states what is known, what is not, and when the next one arrives.

entries.title: Config Drift
entries.productionQuestion: Staging and production behave differently after months of manual changes. How do you find drift?
entries.learningDelta: Drift is inevitable without reconciliation and comparison; config as code plus periodic diff reduces surprise
objectives: Define configuration drift and distinguish it from an intentional environment override.
Explain how manual changes accumulate between reconciliation passes.
Choose a diff and reconciliation cadence that fits the change rate.
Design an audit path that explains a production-only setting.

entries.title: Confluent Cloud Operations
entries.productionQuestion: A managed Kafka cluster shows elevated latency and the app team cannot see brokers. What do you check?
entries.learningDelta: Managed Kafka exposes throughput, partition, and network limits through metrics and quotas; the broker is not yours to tune
objectives: Read cluster and client metrics when broker-level access is unavailable.
Distinguish a quota or partition limit from a network-path latency problem.
Choose a response to a quota breach that does not require tuning a broker.
Explain which limits are cluster-wide and which are client-side.

entries.title: Confused Deputy
entries.productionQuestion: A cross-account role can be assumed by any account that knows its ARN. What condition fixes it?
entries.learningDelta: Confused-deputy protection uses source account, source ARN, or external ID conditions to bind trust to the intended caller
objectives: Explain why a role ARN is not a secret and why a broad trust policy is a confused-deputy risk.
Choose the condition that matches the trust principal: external ID for a third party, source account or ARN for an AWS service.
Detect unauthorized role assumptions and distinguish them from a condition that denies legitimate callers.
Bind a trust policy to the intended caller without breaking the integration.

entries.title: Connection Draining and Deregistration Delay
entries.productionQuestion: A rolling deploy causes 502s even though the new tasks are healthy. What setting do you change?
entries.learningDelta: Deregistration delay lets in-flight requests finish before a target is removed; too short cuts requests, too long slows deploys
objectives: Trace the target lifecycle from deregistration to draining to removal.
Predict 502s from request duration and deregistration delay.
Tune the delay for rollout speed without cutting requests.
Separate draining failures from health-check and capacity failures.

entries.title: Connection Leaks
entries.productionQuestion: The pool is exhausted but request rate is normal. Where did the connections go?
entries.learningDelta: A connection leak holds a session after an error path; pool metrics and stack traces reveal it, but only if timeouts and close paths are correct
objectives: Distinguish a connection leak from a capacity or traffic spike.
Read pool metrics to find connections that never return.
Locate the error path that skips close.
Fix the close path and add detection that catches recurrence.

entries.title: Connection Pools: Queue Before the Database
entries.productionQuestion: The database allows 500 connections and the service has 40 tasks; what pool size?
entries.learningDelta: Pool size is a queueing decision; too small waits, too large multiplies database sessions and contention
objectives: Size a pool from per-task concurrency, query time, and database connection limits.
Separate pool acquisition wait from query execution time using metrics and traces.
Predict when adding pool capacity shifts the bottleneck to the database.
Choose between a client pool and a multiplexing proxy using session-state requirements.

entries.title: Connection Storms
entries.productionQuestion: A network blip causes every app worker to reconnect and mongos CPU spikes. How do you dampen it?
entries.learningDelta: MongoDB drivers pool connections; synchronized reconnects overwhelm mongos and shards without backoff and pool limits
objectives: Explain how per-process connection pools turn a fleet restart into a handshake burst at mongos.
Distinguish connection count, handshake rate, and request rate as separate capacity limits.
Predict when jitter and pool limits dampen a reconnect storm and when they only move the spike.
Size a driver pool and reconnect policy from worker count and mongos capacity.

entries.title: Connection Storms After Failover
entries.productionQuestion: A failover triggers 10k reconnects and the new writer is overwhelmed. How do you dampen it?
entries.learningDelta: Reconnect storms need jitter, backoff, connection pooling, and pre-warmed capacity; immediate retries amplify the failover
objectives: Explain why synchronized reconnects amplify a failover.
Quantify a reconnect burst from client count, jitter, and retry behavior.
Combine pooling, jitter, and backoff instead of relying on one control.
Decide when a proxy is worth the extra network hop.

entries.title: Conntrack Exhaustion: When NAT Forgets
entries.productionQuestion: New connections fail intermittently while established traffic is fine; what table is full?
entries.learningDelta: Conntrack entries track NAT flows; exhaustion and short timeouts drop new connections even when bandwidth is free
objectives: Estimate connection-tracking table occupancy from new-connection rate and entry lifetime.
Tell table exhaustion apart from bandwidth saturation and application errors.
Explain why shortening a timeout can break established flows without freeing the table.
Size or shard NAT capacity and monitor the signals that predict exhaustion.

entries.title: Consistency Models: What a Read Can Promise
entries.productionQuestion: A user updates a profile and immediately sees the old value; which consistency guarantee is missing?
entries.learningDelta: Strong, read-your-writes, monotonic, and eventual consistency are different promises with different costs
objectives: Name the guarantee a user experience actually requires.
Diagnose a stale read from replica lag, routing, and session affinity.
Choose between weakening the promise and routing reads to the primary.
Defend the latency and availability cost of each model.

entries.title: Consumer Groups and Offsets
entries.productionQuestion: A consumer restarts and reprocesses 10 minutes of events. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Offsets are committed by the group; commit interval and processing semantics determine replay and duplicates
objectives: Explain what a committed offset means for a partition and a consumer group.
Distinguish auto-commit from commit-after-processing by its replay and duplicate behavior.
Estimate the replay window from processing rate and commit interval.
Choose a commit policy and duplicate-handling strategy for at-least-once delivery.

entries.title: Consumer Lag: The Real SLO
entries.productionQuestion: Consumer lag is 2 million messages. Is that bad?
entries.learningDelta: Lag must be interpreted with production rate and processing rate; time-to-catch-up is the user-facing signal
objectives: Distinguish lag count, lag age, and time-to-catch-up as different signals.
Compute net drain from production rate and consumer capacity.
Explain why a large lag can be healthy and a small lag can be permanent.
Choose a lag alert and a scaling action from a freshness objective.

entries.title: Container Health Checks
entries.productionQuestion: A task is healthy but not ready, or ready but dead. Which check do you fix?
entries.learningDelta: Container and load balancer health checks answer different questions; liveness restarts, readiness removes traffic
objectives: Separate container health checks from target group health checks by what each one controls.
Predict whether a warm-up will be restarted, removed from traffic, or both.
Tune grace period, interval, and retries from startup time and detection budget.

entries.title: Continuous Profiling: Find the Hot Function
entries.productionQuestion: Latency rose after a release and traces point to one service. Which function is burning CPU?
entries.learningDelta: Continuous profiles aggregate stack samples; flame graphs show self time and call paths that metrics and traces cannot
objectives: Distinguish a service-level CPU rise from the function that consumes the CPU.
Read self time in a flame graph and explain why a waiting span is not a hot frame.
Compare allocation-driven and compute-driven cost in the same profile.
Use a release diff to confirm a regression before changing code.

entries.title: Coordinated Omission: The Metric That Lies
entries.productionQuestion: Your load test reports p99 120ms but users report 4s stalls. What is wrong with the measurement?
entries.learningDelta: Closed-loop generators stop issuing requests during a stall, so slow samples are omitted; latency must be measured against intended arrival time
objectives: Explain how a closed-loop generator omits the requests it failed to send.
Compare reported and intended-arrival latency for the same stall.
Recognize coordinated omission in a load-test result or a metrics pipeline.
Design a load test whose arrival rate and latency correction survive a stall.

entries.title: Cost Allocation
entries.productionQuestion: The bill is one number and no team owns it. How do you allocate cost?
entries.learningDelta: Cost allocation uses tags, accounts, and shared-cost splits; untagged resources and shared platforms need explicit rules
objectives: Separate direct, shared, and untagged spend in a monthly bill.
Explain why tag coverage and shared-cost rules answer different questions.
Diagnose an unowned cost line from allocation rules rather than from the total bill.
Choose an allocation rule and defend its incentives.

entries.title: Cost per Request
entries.productionQuestion: The monthly bill doubled but traffic only grew 20%. What changed per request?
entries.learningDelta: Cost per request separates volume growth from efficiency changes and exposes the expensive path
objectives: Compute cost per request from fixed cost, variable cost, and traffic.
Separate a volume-driven bill increase from a unit-cost increase.
Identify how a shift toward an expensive request path raises unit cost at flat traffic.
Choose the cost metric and breakdown that make the change attributable.

entries.title: Counters, Gauges, and Histograms
entries.productionQuestion: A counter is reset by a deploy and the error graph goes negative. What type or query is wrong?
entries.learningDelta: Counters need rate(), gauges are point-in-time, histograms support quantiles; mixing them produces nonsense
objectives: Match each metric type to the query functions that preserve its meaning.
Explain why a counter reset breaks delta() but not rate().
Tell a counter from a gauge when a value can go down.
Choose between a histogram and a summary for a latency SLO.

entries.title: CPU and Memory Limits
entries.productionQuestion: One task uses all node memory and other tasks are evicted. How do limits work?
entries.learningDelta: Container and task limits bound CPU and memory; reservations influence placement, and exceeding memory leads to OOM
objectives: Distinguish a CPU reservation from a CPU limit and a memory reservation from a hard memory limit.
Predict whether a task is throttled, killed, or left unplaced for a given task size.
Size a task so it protects its neighbors without wasting node capacity.

entries.title: Critical Path: Where the Time Actually Goes
entries.productionQuestion: Service B is slow and Service C is fast, yet C is on the critical path. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Span self-time and waiting time distinguish work from blocked time; the longest span is not always the cause
objectives: Compute the critical path from a span tree with parallel and serial work.
Separate a span's self time from the time it spends waiting on a child.
Predict which optimization lowers end-to-end latency before making it.
Explain why optimizing an off-path span can leave p99 unchanged.

entries.title: Cross-Account Networking
entries.productionQuestion: A shared service must be reachable from five accounts. How do you connect them safely?
entries.learningDelta: Cross-account networking uses resource policies, RAM, and centralized route/security ownership; account boundaries are real trust boundaries
objectives: Separate subnet visibility from service authorization in a shared VPC design.
Compare a named-account share with an organization-wide share and a wildcard resource policy.
Compute the gap between the intended account set and the accounts that can actually reach the service.
Narrow an over-broad share without breaking the five intended consumers.

entries.title: Cross-AZ and Cross-Region Latency
entries.productionQuestion: A service is 30ms slower after moving a dependency to another AZ. Is that expected?
entries.learningDelta: Cross-AZ adds a small latency and transfer cost; cross-region adds much more, and chatty protocols multiply both
objectives: Estimate added latency from placement and the number of serial round trips.
Explain why a chatty protocol turns a small per-hop delay into an SLO breach.
Compare cross-AZ and cross-region transfer cost without treating either as free.
Choose a placement that balances failure isolation, latency, and cost.

entries.title: Cross-AZ Latency and Cost
entries.productionQuestion: The database bill includes a large cross-AZ transfer line. Why is the app talking across zones?
entries.learningDelta: Cross-AZ traffic adds latency and cost; reader placement, chatty queries, and retry loops multiply it
objectives: Trace which application call paths cross an AZ boundary.
Quantify cross-AZ transfer from request rate, round trips, and payload.
Reduce cross-AZ cost without sending every read to the writer.
Explain why the transfer bill can grow faster than request volume.

entries.title: Cross-Cluster Mesh
entries.productionQuestion: A failover sends all traffic to one cluster and latency rises. What does the mesh know?
entries.learningDelta: Cross-cluster mesh discovers remote services; locality and failover policy decide whether traffic stays local
objectives: Explain how a multi-zone control plane makes a remote service discoverable.
Quantify how a failover shift changes local and remote cluster load.
Distinguish remote reachability from remote capacity.
Choose a failover share that fits the remote cluster's headroom.

entries.title: Cross-Region Lag and RPO
entries.productionQuestion: The primary region is failing and replica lag is 90 seconds. How much data do you lose on promotion?
entries.learningDelta: RPO is bounded by replication lag at failover; promotion discards unreplicated writes and requires application reconciliation
objectives: Calculate the data-loss window from replication lag and write rate at the moment of promotion.
Separate RPO from RTO when deciding whether a regional failover is safe.
Explain why a planned switchover can reach RPO 0 while an unplanned failover cannot.
Plan reconciliation for writes the promoted secondary never received.

entries.title: Cross-Zone Load Balancing
entries.productionQuestion: Two AZs have healthy targets, but one AZ gets most traffic. What setting explains it?
entries.learningDelta: Cross-zone balancing distributes across healthy targets in all zones; disabling it isolates zones but can strand capacity
objectives: Explain how a load balancer node chooses targets with cross-zone on and off.
Recognize a per-zone target distribution that is not a health or capacity problem.
Compare zonal isolation, cross-AZ latency, and data-transfer cost.
Choose the cross-zone setting from the failure-domain and capacity requirements.

entries.title: Custom Metric Cost: The Multiplier Stack
entries.productionQuestion: One custom metric across hosts and tags looks cheap in the UI; what does it cost at scale?
entries.learningDelta: Custom metric cost multiplies metric name, hosts, and tag combinations; a small tag change can dominate the bill
objectives: Estimate billable series from metric names, hosts, and tag values before a release.
Explain why submission frequency and query count do not set the custom metric bill.
Find the metric and tag that caused a bill step change.
Propose a tag governance rule that keeps the product question answerable.

entries.title: Customer Communication
entries.productionQuestion: Support is pasting raw incident channel messages to customers. What do you change?
entries.learningDelta: Customer comms need impact, workaround, and next update; internal details and speculation increase harm
objectives: Turn an internal incident state into a customer-facing message.
Include impact, workaround, and next update time in every message.
Remove internal names, hypotheses, and blame before publishing.
Give support one approved statement and a route for follow-up questions.

entries.title: Dark Launches
entries.productionQuestion: The feature must be deployed for weeks before launch. How do you keep it dark?
entries.learningDelta: Dark launches deploy inactive code paths behind flags and verify them with synthetic or internal traffic
objectives: Explain how a dark launch separates deployment from user exposure.
Design a flag default and targeting rule that keeps external users out.
Use internal or synthetic traffic to verify an inactive path.
Recognize the signals that a dark path has become user-visible.

entries.title: Dashboards That Answer One Question
entries.productionQuestion: An on-call engineer opens the dashboard and cannot decide whether to roll back. What is missing?
entries.learningDelta: A dashboard is a decision aid: one question, ordered signals, thresholds, and links to the next check
objectives: Name the single decision a dashboard exists to support.
Order panels by the decision they unblock, not by data availability.
Use thresholds and annotations to make an incident legible at a glance.
Cut panels that add scanning time without changing the decision.

entries.title: Data Classification
entries.productionQuestion: One bucket holds public, internal, and customer data. What is the classification?
entries.learningDelta: Classification drives access, encryption, retention, and incident handling; mixed datasets inherit the highest sensitivity
objectives: Assign a sensitivity label from the data a dataset actually contains.
Explain why a mixed dataset inherits its highest sensitivity.
Trace a classification label to the controls that must follow it.
Find datasets whose controls are weaker than their contents.

entries.title: Data Processing Agreements
entries.productionQuestion: A new SaaS tool will process customer data. What must be agreed before rollout?
entries.learningDelta: A DPA defines processor scope, security, subprocessors, breach notice, and deletion; it is a prerequisite, not paperwork after launch
objectives: Separate the controller's decisions from the processor's obligations in a vendor relationship.
Check whether a DPA covers the legal entity, the specific service, and the data being sent.
Design an onboarding gate that requires an approved agreement and disclosed subprocessors.
Produce evidence that the agreement is operational rather than a signed document in a folder.

entries.title: Data Residency
entries.productionQuestion: A customer contract requires EU-only storage. Which services and logs cross the boundary?
entries.learningDelta: Residency covers storage, processing, support access, backups, and telemetry; a regional bucket does not make the whole path local
objectives: Distinguish a region, an availability zone, and a contractual residency boundary.
Trace storage, processing, backups, telemetry, and support access across a regional path.
Find the global service or control-plane path that a regional data store does not cover.
Design enforcement and evidence for a residency commitment without treating it as a legal opinion.

entries.title: Database Failover and DNS
entries.productionQuestion: The database failed over but the app still writes to the old primary. What did DNS do?
entries.learningDelta: Managed failover updates a DNS name, but client caches, connection pools, and TTLs determine how fast traffic moves
objectives: Trace a writer failover from the database event through DNS resolution and client reconnection.
Explain why a short DNS TTL does not fix a pool that keeps using stale connections.
Estimate time to new writer from DNS TTL, pool recycle time, and reconnect delay.
Reduce failover time without creating a synchronized reconnect storm.

entries.title: Database Failover Incident
entries.productionQuestion: The database fails over and the app takes 10 minutes to recover. What is the sequence?
entries.learningDelta: Failover recovery depends on connection handling, DNS, retries, and capacity; the database may be healthy before the app is
objectives: Sequence a writer failover from detection through application recovery.
Explain why the promoted database can be healthy while the application still fails.
Separate DNS convergence, pool rebuild, and retry amplification in the recovery timeline.
Reduce recovery time by draining, jittering, and bounding reconnects.

entries.title: Datadog Tags and Cardinality
entries.productionQuestion: A new tag contains user IDs and the metric bill tripled. What happened?
entries.learningDelta: Each unique tag combination creates a time series; high-cardinality tags multiply storage, query cost, and billing
objectives: Trace a bill increase to the tag combinations that created new series.
Estimate how a new tag multiplies series from host, endpoint, and value counts.
Separate ingestion volume from indexed series when reading Datadog usage.
Choose a cardinality control that keeps the query the product actually needs.

entries.title: DDoS and Shield: Absorb and Scrub
entries.productionQuestion: Inbound traffic jumps 40× and the load balancer is dropping connections. What absorbs it?
entries.learningDelta: DDoS protection combines edge capacity, anycast scrubbing, and rate controls; origin capacity is not the defense
objectives: Distinguish volumetric, protocol, and application-layer DDoS attacks by the resource they exhaust.
Explain where Shield, anycast, and scrubbing sit relative to the origin.
Choose mitigation controls that match the attack layer and verify the origin is actually protected.

entries.title: Dead Letter Queues
entries.productionQuestion: Failed events go to a DLQ and no one notices for a week. What is missing?
entries.learningDelta: A DLQ is only useful with replay, alerting, ownership, and a retention policy; otherwise it becomes a data dump
objectives: Explain why a DLQ needs an owner and an alert, not just a destination.
Compare DLQ depth with arrival rate and drain time as operating signals.
Recognize the point where retention deletes failures before replay.
Design a replay path that is bounded and verifiable.

entries.title: Debugging 502 Bad Gateway
entries.productionQuestion: Users get 502s and the targets say they are healthy. Where do you look first?
entries.learningDelta: A 502 means the load balancer could not get a valid response from the target; health, protocol, keepalive, and connection reset are the suspects
objectives: Separate an edge-generated 502 from a target-generated 502 using ELB and target metrics and access-log status fields.
Diagnose three target-side causes that can pass a shallow health check: malformed response, connection reset, and TLS handshake failure.
Explain why a health check can stay green while request-path 502s rise.
Choose the first fix from the source instead of adding targets or restarting the fleet.

entries.title: Debugging 503 Service Unavailable
entries.productionQuestion: The ALB returns 503 but CPU is 40%. What are the possible causes?
entries.learningDelta: A 503 can be ELB-generated when no target is registered, or target-generated when a concurrency or pool limit rejects work; CPU alone does not explain it
objectives: Separate an ELB-generated 503 from a target-generated 503 using ELB and target metrics and access-log status fields.
Recognize deregistered or unused targets as an ELB 503 even when target CPU is idle.
Identify a target concurrency or connection-pool limit as a 503 cause at moderate CPU.
Choose between registering capacity, raising a target limit, and shedding load.

entries.title: Debugging 504 Gateway Timeout
entries.productionQuestion: A request returns 504 after 60 seconds; the service logs show 2 seconds of work. Which timeout expired?
entries.learningDelta: A 504 means a timeout expired; it can be generated by the ALB or the target, and the upstream may still be working; align LB, service, and dependency budgets
objectives: Locate which timer expired by comparing client elapsed time, the ALB idle timeout, and the service deadline.
Explain why a service log can show two seconds of work while the client waits sixty seconds.
Distinguish an ALB-generated 504 from a target-generated 504 using access-log and metric signals.
Align load balancer, service, dependency, and retry budgets so the innermost timeout fires first.

entries.title: Decision Logs
entries.productionQuestion: The postmortem cannot explain why the team disabled the breaker. What was missing?
entries.learningDelta: Decision logs record options, rationale, owner, and time; they make incident reconstruction and review possible
objectives: Record the options considered, not only the action taken.
Capture rationale, owner, and time while the decision is fresh.
Use the log to reconstruct a risky action during review.
Explain why a timeline alone cannot explain intent.

entries.title: Degrading in an Incident
entries.productionQuestion: Recommendation latency is causing checkout failures. What do you disable now?
entries.learningDelta: Incident degradation follows a pre-ranked dependency list and feature fallbacks; disabling fast is better than tuning slow
objectives: Rank optional dependencies by their impact on the critical path before an incident.
Choose the smallest set of features to disable to restore checkout.
Explain why a fast, reversible degradation beats latency tuning during an active incident.
Tell customers which features are unavailable without exposing internal details.

entries.title: Dependency Failure
entries.productionQuestion: A payment provider is failing and your service returns 500 for all requests. What do you do?
entries.learningDelta: Dependency failures need isolation, fallback, and clear failure semantics; retrying a third party is not a strategy
objectives: Contain a third-party failure so unrelated flows keep working.
Choose an explicit failure semantic for the affected flow instead of a generic 500.
Explain why retries against a failing provider make containment harder.
Separate the provider's recovery from your service's recovery.

entries.title: Deploying During an Incident
entries.productionQuestion: An incident is active and a fix is ready. Do you deploy now?
entries.learningDelta: Deploys during incidents add variables; prefer reversible config or flags, and deploy only with a clear hypothesis and rollback
objectives: Decide whether a change during an incident is diagnostic, mitigating, or both.
Prefer reversible configuration or flag changes over a broad code deploy.
State the hypothesis and expected signal before changing production.
Bound the added variables with scope and a tested rollback.

entries.title: Deployment Frequency
entries.productionQuestion: The team deploys monthly and every deploy is an incident. What changes first?
entries.learningDelta: Frequent small deploys reduce change size and improve recovery; the constraint is often test and rollback capability, not deploy tooling
objectives: Explain why deploy frequency and change size move together.
Relate batch size to change failure rate and recovery time.
Identify test and rollback capability as the constraint on frequency.
Choose the next improvement when deploys are large and risky.

entries.title: Deployment Verification
entries.productionQuestion: The deploy is green but the checkout path is broken. What verification was missing?
entries.learningDelta: Verification must exercise critical user paths, dependencies, and data, not just process health
objectives: Distinguish process health from verification of a user outcome.
Choose checks that cover critical paths, real dependencies, and data read-back.
Recognize a deployment gate that passes while a critical path is broken.
Block promotion when verification coverage is incomplete.

entries.title: Detecting a Hot Key
entries.productionQuestion: Shard CPU is uneven but no dashboard shows a hot key. How do you find it?
entries.learningDelta: Hot keys are visible in per-key command counts, latency, and shard imbalance; aggregate hit rate hides them
objectives: Tell a hot key from a cluster-wide capacity problem using per-shard and per-key signals.
Explain why aggregate hit rate and cluster average CPU stay healthy during a hot-key incident.
Relate per-key sampling rate to the time needed to attribute a hot key.
Choose a detection method whose sampling cost and blind spots you can defend.

entries.title: Direct Connect
entries.productionQuestion: The office link is down and the VPN backup is not taking traffic. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Direct Connect provides private dedicated connectivity but is not inherently diverse; BGP and backup paths determine failover
objectives: Trace a hybrid path from the office router through a Direct Connect location, virtual interface, and gateway to the VPC.
Distinguish physical diversity from logical failover: two links in one location share a failure domain.
Explain why a VPN that is up can stay unused when the stale Direct Connect route is still preferred.
Choose between restoring the primary path, withdrawing the stale route, and accepting reduced backup capacity.

entries.title: Disk I/O: IOPS, Queue Depth, and fsync
entries.productionQuestion: Disk utilization is 100% and writes take 300ms; is the device slow or overloaded?
entries.learningDelta: IOPS, throughput, and queue depth are different limits; fsync latency exposes durability cost
objectives: Separate an IOPS limit from a throughput limit.
Read queue depth and await together under write pressure.
Explain why fsync latency is a durability signal, not just a slow write.
Choose between more IOPS, more throughput, smaller I/O, and less write amplification.

entries.title: Distributed Tracing: Spans and Causality
entries.productionQuestion: A trace shows 12 spans and the slow one is not the service you expected. How do you read it?
entries.learningDelta: A trace is a causal tree; parent/child timing and span kind reveal where time is spent and where it is waited on
objectives: Read a span tree as causality rather than a flat list of timings.
Use span kind and parent IDs to find where context propagation breaks.
Explain why a missing span hides the real latency contributor.
Choose what to instrument so a trace answers an incident question.

entries.title: DNS Failure
entries.productionQuestion: Nothing resolves and every service looks healthy. How do you confirm DNS?
entries.learningDelta: DNS failures look like many unrelated service failures; resolver, zone, and record health must be checked first
objectives: Recognize a DNS outage disguised as many independent service failures.
Distinguish resolver, authoritative zone, and record failures by their signals.
Use cached-answer coverage and TTL to explain why some clients keep working.
Confirm DNS as the common cause before changing service capacity or deploys.

entries.title: DNS TTL and Failover
entries.productionQuestion: You changed the DNS record but clients still hit the failed region after 10 minutes. Why?
entries.learningDelta: DNS failover is bounded by TTL and resolver caching; applications and JVMs may cache longer than the record TTL
objectives: Compute the stale-answer window from record TTL, resolver caching, detection time, and application cache.
Explain why a DNS change does not move clients that already hold a cached answer or an open connection.
Diagnose a failover that exceeds its recovery objective and reduce the effective cache window safely.

entries.title: DR Drills: Prove RTO and RPO
entries.productionQuestion: The DR plan says 15 minutes RTO. Has anyone measured it?
entries.learningDelta: Untested recovery is a hypothesis; drills measure restore time, data loss, DNS cutover, and application readiness
objectives: Decompose measured RTO into detection, decision, restore, cutover, and application readiness.
Separate the recovery point achieved in a drill from the RPO written in the plan.
Find the unmeasured dependency that lets a database restore pass while the service still fails.
Design a drill that produces evidence without creating a second incident.

entries.title: ECS Deployment Circuit Breaker
entries.productionQuestion: A new task revision fails health checks and the deployment hangs. How do you make ECS roll back?
entries.learningDelta: The deployment circuit breaker detects repeated task failures and can roll back automatically when configured
objectives: Explain what the ECS deployment circuit breaker monitors during a rolling deployment.
Configure automatic rollback and a failure threshold that matches startup behavior.
Distinguish a deployment that is slow from one that is failing and will not recover.
Verify a rollback and the capacity it restores.

entries.title: ECS Exec
entries.productionQuestion: A task is unhealthy but you cannot shell in. How do you inspect it?
entries.learningDelta: ECS Exec uses SSM to run commands in a running task; it requires task role, SSM agent, and audit controls
objectives: List the requirements for ECS Exec: the service flag, the task role, and the SSM agent.
Run a diagnostic command in a live task and preserve an audit record of the session.
Distinguish a missing Exec prerequisite from a missing shell or binary in the container.

entries.title: ECS Logs
entries.productionQuestion: A task was OOM-killed and its container is gone. Where are the logs?
entries.learningDelta: ECS log drivers ship stdout/stderr to CloudWatch or FireLens; task stop reason and previous logs are separate signals
objectives: Follow one task's stdout from the container to CloudWatch Logs or FireLens.
Read a stopped task's stop reason and explain why it can survive missing logs.
Diagnose missing logs from driver, permission, stream, and retention causes.

entries.title: ECS Placement
entries.productionQuestion: All tasks land on one container instance and it saturates. How do you spread them?
entries.learningDelta: Placement strategies and constraints control bin packing and spread; Fargate abstracts instances but not AZ spread
objectives: Compare spread across Availability Zones, spread across instances, and binpack.
Explain why a binding constraint can prevent placement while a strategy only guides it.
Read per-instance utilization instead of trusting the cluster average.
Choose a placement policy that preserves both capacity and Availability Zone spread.

entries.title: ECS Rolling Deployments
entries.productionQuestion: A rolling deployment drops below the minimum healthy percent and causes 503s. What do you check?
entries.learningDelta: minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent control rolling capacity; task draining and health checks determine actual availability
objectives: Calculate the healthy-task floor and surge from minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent.
Predict when a rolling deployment will drop serving capacity below demand.
Separate a stalled rollout from a rollout that is progressing but under capacity.
Explain how health checks and deregistration delay affect whether a new task can serve traffic.

entries.title: ECS Services and Desired Count
entries.productionQuestion: The service says 10 tasks desired but only 6 are running. What does ECS do next?
entries.learningDelta: A service continuously reconciles desired count with running tasks through the scheduler and deployment configuration
objectives: Explain the difference between desired count and running count.
Trace how the service scheduler replaces stopped or unhealthy tasks.
Diagnose a service that cannot reach its desired count because of capacity or health checks.

entries.title: ECS Task Definitions
entries.productionQuestion: A task restarts with different environment variables than the last run. Where do you look?
entries.learningDelta: A task definition is an immutable revision of image, CPU, memory, env, volumes, and IAM; services pin a revision
objectives: Read a task definition revision and identify the image, resource, environment, volume, and role fields.
Explain why a new revision does not change a running service by itself.
Trace a task launch back to the revision that produced its environment.

entries.title: Edge Rate Limiting: Protect the Origin
entries.productionQuestion: One API key sends 80% of requests and the origin is saturated. Where do you limit?
entries.learningDelta: Per-key, per-IP, and global limits solve different abuse; edge limits must account for NAT and shared clients
objectives: Compare per-key, per-IP, and global limits by what they protect and who they punish.
Explain how a shared NAT turns a per-IP limit into collateral damage.
Measure origin load, throttled traffic, and NAT false positives together.
Choose an aggregation key that matches the abusive unit and the client topology.

entries.title: Egress Cost
entries.productionQuestion: The network bill is dominated by data transfer and no one knows which path. How do you attribute it?
entries.learningDelta: Egress costs differ by boundary: AZ, region, internet, and NAT processing; attribution needs flow data and tags
