objectives: Attribute a data-transfer bill to the path that created it, not to the service with the largest total spend.
Compare cross-AZ, cross-region, internet, and NAT processing rates.
Recognize a chatty service-to-service path that dominates cost without a traffic spike.
Choose the cheapest boundary change that preserves latency and resilience.

entries.title: Elections and Availability
entries.productionQuestion: The primary failed and writes failed for 12 seconds. What determines that window?
entries.learningDelta: Elections require a majority and take time; electionTimeout, heartbeat, and catch-up determine write availability
objectives: Break the write outage into detection, election, catch-up, and client discovery.
Explain why a majority of voting members is required and how member loss changes it.
Relate `electionTimeoutMillis`, heartbeats, and catch-up to the observed outage.
Choose a client timeout and retry policy that matches the failover budget.

entries.title: Encryption at Rest and in Transit
entries.productionQuestion: Data is encrypted at rest but crosses a VPC in plaintext. What layer is missing?
entries.learningDelta: Encryption at rest and in transit are separate controls; TLS, mTLS, and service policies cover different paths
objectives: Separate encryption at rest from encryption in transit when auditing a data path.
Identify which hop is unprotected when only one layer is enabled.
Explain what TLS protects and what mutual TLS adds.
Decide when a gap is a key-policy issue and when it is a transport or identity issue.

entries.title: Envoy Admin and Stats
entries.productionQuestion: A request fails and the app has no error. What does Envoy admin show?
entries.learningDelta: Envoy admin exposes config dump, clusters, stats, and readiness; it is the fastest way to see proxy-level state
objectives: Name the admin endpoint that answers a proxy-level question.
Distinguish an application error from a request that never reached the application.
Read cluster health and upstream failure counters without guessing.
Use readiness and config dump to confirm what the proxy actually loaded.

entries.title: Envoy Clusters and Endpoints
entries.productionQuestion: The mesh reports no healthy upstreams while pods are running. Which cluster view do you check?
entries.learningDelta: Envoy clusters group endpoints and health; outlier ejection and endpoint discovery determine usable capacity
objectives: Separate cluster membership from endpoint health and usable capacity.
Explain how endpoint discovery, active health checks, and outlier ejection change the load-balancing set.
Read the cluster signals that distinguish missing endpoints from ejected endpoints.
Choose an ejection cap that protects capacity without hiding a failing dependency.

entries.title: Envoy Listeners
entries.productionQuestion: A request never reaches the service. Which Envoy listener should have accepted it?
entries.learningDelta: Envoy listeners bind addresses and ports and pass connections into filter chains and route configuration
objectives: Trace a connection through listener, filter chain, HTTP connection manager, route, and cluster.
Distinguish a port with no listener from a listener whose filter chain does not match.
Read listener-level evidence to decide whether a failure is below or above HTTP.

entries.title: Envoy Retry Storm
entries.productionQuestion: A dependency fails for 5 seconds and request volume triples for 5 minutes. What caused it?
entries.learningDelta: Coordinated proxy retries amplify failure; retry budgets, jitter, and circuit breaking bound the amplification
objectives: Distinguish a dependency fault from the retry amplification that follows it.
Calculate how attempts, retry budgets, and breakers change offered load.
Explain why a jittered retry policy still produces a sustained storm.
Choose a retry control whose fail-fast tradeoff you can defend.

entries.title: Envoy Routes
entries.productionQuestion: A canary route works for one header but all traffic hits the stable version. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Routes match in order; host/path/header predicates and route order decide which cluster receives traffic
objectives: Explain how Envoy selects a virtual host and then the first matching route.
Predict which cluster receives traffic when a broad route is placed before a specific route.
Read a route table and a weighted-cluster split without confusing weight with match precedence.

entries.title: Error Budget Policy
entries.productionQuestion: The error budget is exhausted but the roadmap says ship. Who decides?
entries.learningDelta: An error budget policy pre-agrees consequences and exceptions; without it, the budget is only a dashboard
objectives: Distinguish an error budget from an error budget policy.
Write a policy with a trigger, a consequence, an exception path, and an owner.
Explain why an exception needs a decision, a time limit, and a record.
Defend a release freeze without turning the policy into an absolute ban.

entries.title: Error Tracking: Grouping and Fingerprints
entries.productionQuestion: One error group has 40k events and three unrelated root causes. How do you split it?
entries.learningDelta: Error grouping uses fingerprints; stable, specific fingerprints preserve distinct causes without exploding issue count
objectives: Explain how a fingerprint turns many error events into one issue.
Choose fingerprint inputs that separate causes without multiplying noise.
Diagnose a new error class buried inside an existing group.
Triage an error stream by cause and release rather than by raw event count.

entries.title: Escalation
entries.productionQuestion: The on-call engineer is stuck and 30 minutes pass before backup is called. How do you escalate sooner?
entries.learningDelta: Escalation paths and triggers remove the social cost of asking; time-based and impact-based triggers work together
objectives: Distinguish a time-based escalation trigger from an impact-based one.
Explain why explicit authority shortens time to backup.
Design an escalation path that names who is called, when, and with what context.
Recognize over-escalation and false pages as costs, not free insurance.

entries.title: Eviction Policies: Protect the Working Set
entries.productionQuestion: Redis is at maxmemory and hit rate collapses. Which keys are being evicted?
entries.learningDelta: allkeys policies may evict hot data; volatile policies only evict keys with TTL; policy must match the cache's purpose
objectives: Predict which keys an eviction policy can remove under memory pressure.
Tell a falling hit rate from rejected writes as the failure signal.
Choose between allkeys and volatile policies from the key mix.
Size maxmemory with headroom for the working set and buffers.

entries.title: Evidence Collection
entries.productionQuestion: The audit starts tomorrow and evidence lives in screenshots. How do you prepare?
entries.learningDelta: Evidence should be generated continuously from systems of record with timestamps, ownership, and retention
objectives: Distinguish evidence produced by an operating control from a screenshot assembled after the fact.
Design an evidence pipeline that captures scope, timestamp, owner, and source for every sample.
Match retention to the audit window and test the lifecycle policy before it deletes proof.
Prepare a defensible evidence set without turning audit preparation into a manual scramble.

entries.title: Exactly-Once Semantics
entries.productionQuestion: Kafka is configured for exactly-once, but the sink still has duplicates. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Kafka transactions make broker writes atomic; end-to-end exactly-once requires idempotent sinks or transactional outputs
objectives: Separate broker-level exactly-once guarantees from the effect a sink applies.
Trace how a retry after a sink write creates a duplicate even when Kafka transactions are enabled.
Choose between an idempotent sink and a transactional output for a given downstream system.
Name the latency and operational costs that end-to-end exactly-once adds.

entries.title: Exemplars: From Metric to Trace
entries.productionQuestion: p99 is high and you need one concrete slow request. How do you get from the graph to the trace?
entries.learningDelta: Exemplars attach trace IDs to metric samples, connecting aggregates to individual requests without storing every trace
objectives: Explain what an exemplar stores and why it is not a substitute for a histogram bucket.
Trace a slow bucket to a sampled request and name the two conditions that must both hold.
Diagnose a missing exemplar without blaming the histogram or the query.
Choose a trace sample rate that preserves links for the investigations you support.

entries.title: Expand/Contract Migrations
entries.productionQuestion: A column rename breaks the previous release. How do you sequence it?
entries.learningDelta: Expand/contract adds the new shape, backfills, dual-writes, then removes the old shape; each step is independently deployable
objectives: Break a schema rename into expand, backfill, dual-write, and contract steps.
Explain why each step must be independently deployable and reversible.
Detect an incomplete backfill before it reaches new readers.
Decide when the old code is drained enough to run the contract step.

entries.title: Failure Domains: Blast Radius by Design
entries.productionQuestion: A single rack failure took down the service despite three AZs; what was correlated?
entries.learningDelta: Independent failure domains require independent power, network, deployment, and dependency paths, not just AZ labels
objectives: Distinguish an availability zone from an independent failure domain.
Find correlated dependencies that defeat zonal redundancy.
Estimate blast radius from domain scope and replication.
Challenge a redundancy claim with a failure test that crosses domain boundaries.

entries.title: Fargate Cold Starts
entries.productionQuestion: Autoscaling adds tasks but p99 still spikes for two minutes. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Fargate tasks need scheduling, image pull, startup, and health check time before serving; scaling must anticipate it
objectives: Break a Fargate cold start into scheduling, image pull, application startup, and health-check phases.
Predict whether a scale-out can become serving capacity before a known traffic spike.
Distinguish a scaling decision that is too late from one that is correct but blocked by startup time.
Reduce the gap with earlier scaling, faster startup, or warm capacity.

entries.title: Fargate Spot
entries.productionQuestion: Fargate Spot is cheaper but tasks disappear. Which workloads fit?
entries.learningDelta: Fargate Spot uses spare capacity with interruption notices; stateless, retryable, and drained workloads tolerate it
objectives: Explain how Fargate Spot interruptions arrive and how much notice the task gets.
Keep a minimum healthy floor on Fargate while sending flexible work to Fargate Spot.
Tune graceful shutdown so an interruption does not cut in-flight work.
Decide which workloads are interruption-tolerant and which need on-demand capacity.

entries.title: Feature Flags
entries.productionQuestion: The code is deployed but the feature must stay off for one tenant. What do you use?
entries.learningDelta: Flags separate deploy from release; flag scope, defaults, and cleanup determine safety and long-term risk
objectives: Explain the difference between deploying code and releasing a feature.
Predict exposure from a flag default, targeting rules, and percentage rollout.
Recognize why a default-on flag is global exposure, not a safe fallback.
Design flag ownership, kill switches, and cleanup to limit long-term risk.

entries.title: File Descriptors: The Invisible Capacity Limit
entries.productionQuestion: The service is healthy but new connections fail with “too many open files”; where do you look?
entries.learningDelta: Every socket and file consumes an fd; per-process and system limits turn leaks into hard failures
objectives: Explain how sockets, files, and epoll registrations consume file descriptors.
Distinguish a descriptor leak from a traffic spike using the fd count and its slope.
Choose between fixing the close path and raising the limit, and state the tradeoff.
Read the signals that separate fd exhaustion from CPU or memory saturation.

entries.title: Game Days
entries.productionQuestion: The team knows the system but has never practiced an incident together. What does a game day test?
entries.learningDelta: Game days combine a realistic scenario, roles, communications, and a debrief; they test people and process as much as technology
objectives: Design a game day scenario with realistic injects and a clear scope.
Assign roles that separate command, operations, communications, and record-keeping.
Explain why a debrief with owners matters more than the failure itself.
Recognize the coordination gaps a game day exposes before a real incident does.

entries.title: GDPR for Engineers
entries.productionQuestion: A user asks for their data. Which systems must answer?
entries.learningDelta: GDPR rights require data discovery, deletion, export, and lawful basis across primary stores, caches, logs, and backups
objectives: Translate data-subject rights into discovery, export, correction, and deletion operations across every store.
Find the systems that make a request incomplete even when the primary database reports success.
Separate a documented lawful basis from the engineering controls that enforce purpose and retention.
Scope a rights-readiness review without treating it as a legal opinion.

entries.title: GitOps
entries.productionQuestion: A manual console change disappears on the next sync. Why?
entries.learningDelta: GitOps makes Git the desired state; drift reconciliation overwrites manual changes, which is safety and a trap
objectives: Explain desired state, reconciliation, and drift in a GitOps controller.
Predict when a manual console change is reverted.
Distinguish safe drift correction from an automated revert during an incident.
Design an expedited Git path and a bounded reconciliation pause for emergencies.

entries.title: Global Accelerator: Anycast for Your ALBs
entries.productionQuestion: Users on another continent see 300ms extra and DNS failover is too slow. What does Global Accelerator change?
entries.learningDelta: Global Accelerator uses anycast IPs and AWS backbone to reach regional endpoints; it removes DNS TTL from the failover path
objectives: Explain how Global Accelerator combines anycast entry, AWS backbone, and health-checked endpoint groups.
Compare Global Accelerator failover with DNS failover for latency, client caching, and connection behavior.
Diagnose a deployment that still waits on DNS because clients bypass the accelerator.

entries.title: Golden Signals: Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation
entries.productionQuestion: CPU is normal, the dashboard is green, and users are complaining. Which signal did you not graph?
entries.learningDelta: The four golden signals answer different questions; saturation can hide while latency, errors, or traffic already show the incident
objectives: Read latency, traffic, errors, and saturation as four different questions.
Explain why a healthy CPU graph can coexist with a failing request path.
Separate failed-request latency from successful-request latency.
Choose the first signal to graph for a service incident and defend the coverage gap.

entries.title: Graceful Degradation: Cut Features, Keep Promises
entries.productionQuestion: Recommendations are down and the product is timing out; what do you disable first?
entries.learningDelta: Degradation is a designed dependency hierarchy; non-critical work must fail without taking the core path
objectives: Rank dependencies by what the product promises, not by how visible they are.
Separate an optional call's timeout and failure path from the critical request budget.
Design a fallback that is useful, bounded, and honest about being degraded.
Explain why a 200 response with a missing module can be better than a 500.

entries.title: gRPC Load Balancing
entries.productionQuestion: gRPC clients pin to one backend despite many replicas. Why?
entries.learningDelta: gRPC uses long-lived HTTP/2 connections; connection-level balancing pins streams, so request-level or proxy balancing is required
objectives: Explain why a Layer 4 load balancer chooses a backend once per HTTP/2 connection.
Relate client count, backend count, and stream concurrency to load skew.
Compare connection-level, proxy, and client-side gRPC balancing.
Choose a balancing design from connection count, latency, and operational cost.

entries.title: Head Sampling: Cheap and Blind
entries.productionQuestion: A 5% head sample makes a rare error class invisible. What is the tradeoff?
entries.learningDelta: Head sampling decides before the request outcome is known; it is cheap and unbiased for volume but unreliable for rare outcomes
objectives: Explain why a head sampler cannot select a trace by its eventual error or latency.
Estimate captured error spans from request rate, error share, sampling rate, and window.
Read a blind-spot probability instead of trusting a low sampled error count.
Choose a sampling rate that fits a span budget and state what it cannot answer.

entries.title: Health Checks: Fast Detection vs Flapping
entries.productionQuestion: A single slow health check removed every task at once. What settings caused it?
entries.learningDelta: Interval, timeout, healthy/unhealthy thresholds, and grace period trade detection speed against false positives
objectives: Calculate detection and recovery time from health-check settings.
Explain why a shared dependency can remove every target at once.
Tune thresholds to survive a transient blip without hiding a real failure.
Place the grace period at the orchestrator, not the target group.

entries.title: HIPAA for Engineers
entries.productionQuestion: A health-data workload needs HIPAA readiness. Which controls are actually required?
entries.learningDelta: HIPAA requires administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for protected health information; engineering owns access, audit, integrity, and transmission controls
objectives: Separate the Security Rule's administrative, physical, and technical safeguards and identify which ones engineering implements directly.
Evaluate a health-data workload against access, audit, integrity, authentication, and transmission controls.
Recognize when a control exists but its evidence is too stale to demonstrate operation.
Scope a HIPAA readiness review without treating it as a legal opinion.

entries.title: Histogram Quantiles: Buckets Decide the Tail
entries.productionQuestion: The p99 panel says 200ms but traces show 2s requests. Which is wrong?
entries.learningDelta: Histogram quantiles are interpolated within buckets; poor bucket layout hides the tail and cannot exceed the largest bucket
objectives: Explain how histogram_quantile interpolates inside a bucket.
Predict when a tail is invisible because it falls below the requested quantile.
Recognize a p99 clamped by the highest finite bucket.
Choose a bucket layout or native histogram for the tail you need to see.

entries.title: Host and Path Routing
entries.productionQuestion: You need to route api.meridian.internal and app.meridian.internal to different services. Where does routing belong?
entries.learningDelta: Host/path routing at the ALB is cheap and centralized; it must account for certificates, wildcard scope, and rule limits
objectives: Place host and path routing at a layer that can see the HTTP request.
Explain how SNI and certificate scope interact with host rules.
Diagnose a TLS failure that happens before any routing rule runs.
Design tenant routing with certificate coverage and rule limits in mind.

entries.title: Hot Key Sharding: One Key, One Saturated Shard
entries.productionQuestion: One Redis key is getting 40% of traffic. Seven shards are idle and one is on fire. What do you do?
entries.learningDelta: A hot key is a partitioning problem; salting, local caching, and read replicas solve different parts of it, and resizing the cache does not
objectives: Tell a hot key from a cluster-wide capacity problem using per-shard signals.
Compare local caching, key salting, and read replicas by failure mode and tradeoff.
Explain why aggregate hit rate and average CPU can hide a saturated shard.
Choose a mitigation whose staleness, lag, and migration cost you can defend.

entries.title: Hot Partitions
entries.productionQuestion: One tenant's partition receives 60% of writes and its disk is full. What do you do?
entries.learningDelta: A hot partition is a data-distribution problem; splitting the key or isolating the tenant changes the balance and the operational model
objectives: Measure skew as the hottest partition against the median, not the cluster average.
Explain why adding partitions does not split one tenant's key range.
Choose between key spreading, tenant isolation, and archival for a hot partition.
Predict which capacity limit binds when one partition saturates.

entries.title: Hot Shard in Redis Cluster
entries.productionQuestion: One hash slot is saturated while the cluster has free capacity. Can you move the slot?
entries.learningDelta: Redis Cluster distributes keys by hash slot; a hot key and its co-located keys share a shard, and resharding cannot split one key
objectives: Explain how a key maps to a hash slot and a shard in Redis Cluster.
Separate moving a slot from splitting the traffic inside it.
Predict what resharding changes when one slot owns most of the load.
Choose a fix that reduces hot-slot load rather than moving it.

entries.title: Hot Shards
entries.productionQuestion: One shard has 80% CPU and the others are idle. Is the balancer broken?
entries.learningDelta: The balancer moves chunks, but a hot key within a chunk or a monotonically increasing key can keep one shard hot
objectives: Diagnose a hot shard from per-shard CPU and write rate while chunk counts look balanced.
Explain why moving or splitting chunks does not split one key's traffic.
Distinguish a key-distribution hotspot from a balancer that is disabled or behind.
Choose a fix that changes the key distribution rather than only moving the same load.

entries.title: HTTP/2 and Keep-Alive: Reuse With Rules
entries.productionQuestion: The load balancer is healthy but backends see a new connection per request; why?
entries.learningDelta: Connection reuse depends on both peers agreeing on idle timeouts, max requests, and protocol; mismatches cause churn
objectives: Explain how idle timeouts, request caps, and protocol choice decide connection reuse.
Find the peer whose timeout closes a connection first.
Diagnose connection churn from client, load balancer, and backend metrics together.
Align connection lifetimes without creating reconnect storms during deploys.

entries.title: HTTP/3 and QUIC
entries.productionQuestion: Mobile users on lossy networks see slow loads over TCP. Would QUIC help, and what breaks?
entries.learningDelta: QUIC runs over UDP with independent streams and faster handshakes; loss affects streams differently but UDP may be blocked
objectives: Explain how QUIC removes TCP head-of-line blocking without making loss free.
Compare HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 latency under packet loss and round-trip time.
Predict what happens when a network blocks UDP and fallback is missing.
Design an HTTP/3 rollout with a safe HTTP/2 fallback path.

entries.title: IAM Roles and Trust
entries.productionQuestion: A service uses an access key in an environment variable. What replaces it?
entries.learningDelta: IAM roles use trust policies and temporary credentials; the workload assumes a role instead of storing keys
objectives: Separate a role's trust policy from its permission policy and explain what each one decides.
Trace a workload credential from an instance profile or OIDC token through STS to a role session.
Recognise an over-broad trust policy as an exposure even when the workload still works.
Choose the smallest change that removes a static key without breaking the service.

entries.title: Idempotency: Retries Without Duplicate Side Effects
entries.productionQuestion: The payment timed out; did it charge the customer, and is it safe to retry?
entries.learningDelta: An idempotency key makes a retried write return the original result instead of creating a second effect
objectives: Explain why an ambiguous timeout makes a write unsafe to retry without a key.
Design an idempotency key store with a reservation, a stored response, and a retention window.
Distinguish at-least-once delivery from exactly-once effects.
Choose a dedupe window and concurrency behavior that match the retry path.

entries.title: Idempotent Producer
entries.productionQuestion: A producer retries a batch and the consumer sees duplicates. What fixes it?
entries.learningDelta: Idempotent producers use sequence numbers and producer IDs to deduplicate retries within a session
objectives: Explain how an ambiguous acknowledgement turns a retry into a duplicate record.
Describe how a producer ID and per-partition sequence number let the broker drop a retried batch.
Distinguish idempotent retry suppression from application-level and cross-session duplicate handling.
Choose idempotence and in-flight settings that preserve ordering without hiding duplicates.

entries.title: Image Pull and Registry Limits
entries.productionQuestion: New tasks take 90 seconds to start and the registry is throttling. What do you change?
entries.learningDelta: Image size, layers, cache, and registry pull limits determine task startup; a large image multiplies cold-start cost
objectives: Explain how image size, layer count, and concurrent pulls affect time to ready.
Predict when a shared registry budget will throttle a deployment.
Distinguish registry throttling from application startup and health-check delay.
Reduce startup time with smaller images, fewer layers, or a different pull strategy.

entries.title: Immutable Artifacts
entries.productionQuestion: Staging passed but production runs a different build. What went wrong?
entries.learningDelta: Immutable artifacts are built once, identified by digest, and promoted; rebuilding per environment changes the software
objectives: Explain why rebuilding per environment produces different software from the same commit.
Use an image digest rather than a mutable tag as the deployment identity.
Identify the controls that prove staging and production ran the same bits.
Design a promotion and retention path that keeps rollback artifacts available.

entries.title: Incident Checklists
entries.productionQuestion: During a failover the team forgets to disable the retry storm. What prevents that?
entries.learningDelta: Checklists reduce omission under stress; they must be short, ordered, and tied to verification
objectives: Explain why a short, ordered checklist beats a long procedure under stress.
Identify the steps whose omission creates a second outage rather than a delay.
Design read-back verification that proves a step happened.
Recognize when checklist length itself increases the chance of omission.

entries.title: Incident Command
entries.productionQuestion: Five engineers are debugging and no one is communicating. What role is missing?
entries.learningDelta: Incident command assigns one coordinator, one communications owner, and one operations owner so investigation and communication do not compete
objectives: Explain what an incident commander owns, and what that role does not own.
Separate the command, operations, and communications responsibilities during an active incident.
Recognize parallel debugging as a coordination failure, not a staffing shortage.
Choose the smallest command structure that fits the incident's impact and duration.

entries.title: Incident Notification Timelines
entries.productionQuestion: A breach is suspected at 02:00. When does the notification clock start?
entries.learningDelta: Notification deadlines vary by regulation and jurisdiction; legal must be engaged as soon as a reportable incident is suspected
objectives: Explain when a notification clock starts and why a completed investigation is not required first.
Select the applicable deadline from the regime, recipient, and contract instead of assuming a universal value.
Compare a 24-hour contractual window, the GDPR 72-hour timeline, and a 60-day outer limit.
Design a notification record that states what is known, what is still being assessed, and when the decision was made.

entries.title: Incident Review
entries.productionQuestion: The review becomes a debate about who caused it. How do you run it?
entries.learningDelta: Incident reviews examine timeline, contributing factors, and actions; facilitation and blameless framing keep the focus on systems
objectives: Facilitate a review that follows evidence instead of the loudest theory.
Keep discussion at the level of conditions and decisions under uncertainty.
Convert disagreement into a recorded open question or a systemic action.
Close the review with actions that match the contributing factors.

entries.title: Incident Roles
entries.productionQuestion: The database expert is also writing customer updates and misses the fix. How do you staff the incident?
entries.learningDelta: Separate command, operations, communications, and subject-matter roles; one person may hold two only in small incidents
objectives: Distinguish a role from the person currently filling it.
Recognize when a subject-matter expert is being consumed by coordination work.
Staff an incident from the roles the response needs, not from who is available first.
Decide when to combine roles and when the combination becomes the failure.

entries.title: Incident Timeline
entries.productionQuestion: Two teams disagree about when the rollback happened. How do you settle it?
entries.learningDelta: A timeline combines alerts, deploys, decisions, and communications with synchronized timestamps and sources
objectives: Build one incident chronology from alerts, deploys, decisions, and communications.
Label each entry with its source and the basis for its timestamp.
Resolve disagreements by comparing clocks and recording the remaining uncertainty.
Explain why clock skew can make a cause look like an effect.

entries.title: Index Design
entries.productionQuestion: A compound index is not used even though its fields appear in the query. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Index field order, sort direction, and predicate shape determine whether MongoDB can use an index efficiently
objectives: Read a compound index as an ordered list of keys, not a set of fields.
Apply the equality-sort-range guideline to a query shape.
Explain why an index whose fields all appear in a query can still be bypassed.
Use scanned-document counts and explain output to validate a plan.

entries.title: Indexing: The Right Index for the Query
entries.productionQuestion: A query is slow and adding an index doubles write latency. What do you check?
entries.learningDelta: Indexes trade read speed for write cost and space; the query plan, selectivity, and column order decide whether an index helps
objectives: Predict whether a B-tree index can serve a predicate from its shape, not its name.
Explain why a function on the indexed column makes a predicate non-sargable.
Quantify the write and storage cost of each additional index on a write-heavy table.
Choose between a composite, partial, or covering index for a specific query.

entries.title: Ingress Gateway
entries.productionQuestion: External traffic bypasses mesh policy and reaches pods directly. What do you change?
entries.learningDelta: An ingress gateway provides a controlled entry point with TLS, routing, and policy; bypass paths defeat mTLS and observability
objectives: Explain what an ingress gateway adds at the mesh edge beyond a load balancer.
Trace an external request through the gateway and identify a bypass path.
Choose TLS and policy controls that cover every external entry point.
Size gateway capacity for the traffic that actually reaches it.

entries.title: Internet Gateway
entries.productionQuestion: A public subnet has a 0.0.0.0/0 route but still no internet. What is missing?
entries.learningDelta: An internet gateway attaches to the VPC and requires public IPs, routes, and security groups to work together
objectives: Explain what an internet gateway attaches to and what it does for IPv4 and IPv6.
Check the full public path: address, security group, route, and gateway attachment.
Separate a missing gateway, a missing route, a missing public address, and a blocking rule.
Choose between an internet gateway, a NAT gateway, and an egress-only internet gateway.

entries.title: ISO 27001
entries.productionQuestion: The ISO audit finds policies but no risk treatment. What is missing?
entries.learningDelta: ISO 27001 requires a risk-based management system with ownership, treatment plans, and continual improvement
objectives: Distinguish an information security management system from a document set.
Trace a high risk from assessment through an owned, approved treatment.
Identify the evidence an internal audit and management review must produce.
Prioritize remediation when the risk register and treatment plan disagree.

entries.title: Kafka Hot Partition
entries.productionQuestion: One partition is at 100% and the others are idle because one key is 60% of traffic. What do you do?
entries.learningDelta: Hot partitions come from key skew; salting, key redesign, or splitting the event changes ordering and consumer logic
objectives: Diagnose a hot partition from per-partition load and lag rather than topic averages.
Explain why more consumers or more partitions do not split one key by themselves.
Compare salting, key redesign, event splitting, and partition changes by ordering cost.
Choose a fix and a migration sequence that keeps consumers correct during rollout.

entries.title: Kafka ISR and Under-Replicated Partitions
entries.productionQuestion: One broker is down and partitions are under-replicated. Are writes still safe?
entries.learningDelta: ISR tracks in-sync replicas; min.insync.replicas and acks determine whether writes continue and whether durability is reduced
objectives: Read the in-sync replica set and under-replicated partition count together.
Predict write acceptance when ISR falls below min.insync.replicas.
Distinguish availability from durability when writes continue.
Choose a response that restores replication before the next failure.

entries.title: Kafka Partitions: The Unit of Parallelism
entries.productionQuestion: A topic has 12 partitions and 20 consumers. Why are 8 consumers idle?
entries.learningDelta: A partition is consumed by one consumer per group; partition count caps consumer parallelism and sets ordering scope
objectives: Explain why a consumer group assigns at most one consumer per partition.
Calculate a topic's throughput ceiling from partition count and per-consumer capacity.
Diagnose idle consumers and growing lag from assignment and per-partition load.
Choose between more partitions, more consumers, and faster consumers.

entries.title: Kafka Transactions
entries.productionQuestion: A consumer writes output and commits its offset separately, causing duplicates. How do transactions help?
entries.learningDelta: Transactions atomically commit produced records and consumed offsets, but add latency and require transactional consumers
objectives: Explain the crash window between an output write and an offset commit.
Describe how sendOffsetsToTransaction makes both writes atomic.
Recognize the latency and isolation-level costs of transactions.
Decide when a transaction is needed and when an idempotent sink is enough.

entries.title: Keep-Alive and Idle Timeout Mismatch
entries.productionQuestion: The ALB opens a new backend connection for almost every request. Which timeout is misaligned?
entries.learningDelta: Keep-alive must outlive the load balancer's idle timeout; if the backend closes first, requests race and connections churn
objectives: Compare the load balancer idle timeout with the backend keep-alive timeout.
Explain why a backend that closes first creates both churn and 502 responses.
Diagnose the race from connection counts and 502s rather than target health.
Choose which timeout to change and state the cost of the choice.

entries.title: Key Salting: Spread One Key Across Shards
entries.productionQuestion: Salting a key spreads load but changes every reader. How do you migrate safely?
entries.learningDelta: Salting adds a deterministic suffix to fan a hot key across shards; it requires reading all salted variants and a migration plan
objectives: Design a deterministic salt scheme that changes the hash slot of each variant.
Explain how fan-out reads multiply work even when writes are spread.
Sequence a migration that keeps unsalted readers correct during the transition.
Choose between dual-write, dual-read, and a bounded shadow migration for a write-hot key.

entries.title: Keys and Ordering
entries.productionQuestion: Two updates for one order arrive out of order. What key should the producer use?
entries.learningDelta: Kafka preserves order within a partition; keying by entity keeps its events ordered while allowing parallelism across keys
objectives: Map an event key to a partition and state the ordering scope it creates.
Choose a key that preserves per-entity order without collapsing the topic to one partition.
Recognize when a coarse key trades ordering for partition skew.
Diagnose out-of-order events from partition assignment, not consumer timing.

entries.title: KMS and Envelope Encryption
entries.productionQuestion: Each S3 object is encrypted with a KMS key and latency rises. What is the better pattern?
entries.learningDelta: Envelope encryption uses a data key for bulk data and KMS to protect the data key; direct KMS calls are for small secrets
objectives: Trace a direct KMS call and an envelope-encrypted write end to end.
Explain why bulk data uses a data key while KMS protects that key.
Recognize KMS request throttling from latency and error signals before storage throughput is blamed.
Choose a data-key reuse and caching strategy that keeps the key policy and rotation requirements intact.

entries.title: ksqlDB Queries and State
entries.productionQuestion: A ksqlDB query restarts and takes 20 minutes to catch up. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Stateful queries rebuild state stores from the changelog; restart time depends on state size and changelog throughput
objectives: Explain why a stateful query must rebuild its state store before it can process new input.
Estimate restart time from state size, restore throughput, and task count.
Distinguish restore time from input backlog catch-up time.
Choose a mitigation that reduces recovery time without breaking correctness.

entries.title: Kuma Control Plane
entries.productionQuestion: A policy applies to half the mesh and no one knows why. Where is the selector?
entries.learningDelta: Kuma's control plane distributes policies to selected data plane proxies; selectors, mesh scope, and versions decide where they apply
objectives: Separate control plane configuration from data plane traffic handling.
Trace a Kuma policy from its selector to the data plane proxies that receive it.
Diagnose a policy that overmatches, misses, or never reaches its intended workloads.

entries.title: L4 vs L7: Choose the Right Load Balancer
entries.productionQuestion: You need static IPs and millions of connections, but also path routing. Which layer do you choose?
entries.learningDelta: L4 routes connections and cannot inspect paths; L7 routes requests and terminates protocols; the correct design often layers both
objectives: Distinguish connection-level forwarding from request-level routing.
Map static IP, throughput, and path-routing requirements to a load balancer layer.
Explain why a Layer 4 load balancer cannot evaluate an HTTP path.
Design an NLB-to-ALB chain that keeps static IPs and path rules.

entries.title: Lead Time for Changes
entries.productionQuestion: A one-line fix takes two weeks to reach production. Where is the time spent?
entries.learningDelta: Lead time is dominated by queues, approvals, and test duration; optimize the constraint, not the average
objectives: Break lead time into coding, queue, test, and deployment components.
Identify the constraint that dominates a slow change.
Explain why optimizing a non-constraint does not reduce lead time.
Choose a change that shortens the queue without removing safety.

entries.title: Least Privilege
entries.productionQuestion: A task role has `*:*` and security wants it reduced. How do you find the real permissions?
entries.learningDelta: Least privilege starts from observed access, uses scoped resources and conditions, and is verified in a non-production environment
objectives: Read an identity policy by action, resource, and condition instead of by action name alone.
Use observed access to shrink a broad role without blocking a production path.
Separate a missing permission from a resource-scope or condition mismatch.
Decide when a scoped policy is safe to ship and how to verify it before production.

entries.title: Legal and Compliance During Incidents
entries.productionQuestion: A breach may have exposed customer data. Who decides notification?
entries.learningDelta: Incident response must include legal and privacy counsel when data, contracts, or regulated data may be affected; deadlines start early
objectives: Decide when an incident needs legal and privacy counsel in the response.
Preserve evidence and control disclosure while the technical response continues.
Track notification obligations from first awareness rather than confirmed root cause.
Explain why the legal workstream runs in parallel with mitigation, not after it.

entries.title: Linux CPU Saturation: Run Queue and Steal
entries.productionQuestion: CPU is at 60% but latency is high; is the host actually saturated?
entries.learningDelta: Run-queue length, steal time, and per-core saturation reveal CPU pressure that a smoothed utilization average hides
objectives: Distinguish guest CPU utilization from available CPU capacity.
Read run queue, load average, steal, and iowait without conflating them.
Explain why a host at moderate CPU can still queue requests.
Choose between adding vCPUs, moving the workload, or reducing concurrency.

entries.title: Linux Memory: Page Cache, RSS, and OOM
entries.productionQuestion: The host reports 90% memory used but nothing is swapping; is it about to OOM?
entries.learningDelta: Page cache is reclaimable; anonymous memory, kernel memory, and cgroup limits decide OOM behavior
objectives: Separate anonymous memory from reclaimable page cache.
Read a cgroup limit, usage, and pressure signal together.
Predict when the kernel reclaims and when the OOM killer runs.
Choose between reducing the working set and raising the limit.

entries.title: Little's Law: Concurrency, Latency, Throughput
entries.productionQuestion: Throughput is flat and latency is rising: how much concurrency is actually in the system?
entries.learningDelta: L = λW ties concurrency, arrival rate, and time in system; rising latency at fixed throughput means work is piling up
objectives: Use L = λW to estimate in-flight work from throughput and latency.
Tell a throughput problem from a concurrency or capacity problem.
Explain why a queue grows without bound once arrivals exceed service capacity.
Size a concurrency limit or worker pool from a latency and throughput target.

entries.title: Load Shedding in an Incident
entries.productionQuestion: The service is overloaded and every request is timing out. What do you shed first?
entries.learningDelta: Incident load shedding is a product decision made in advance: protect the critical path, drop low-value work, and communicate
objectives: Choose what to shed first using a pre-agreed ranking of request classes.
Explain why protecting the critical path matters more than preserving total request count.
Recognize the moment when shedding everything is the same failure as shedding nothing.
Write the customer-facing message that accompanies a shedding decision.

entries.title: Load Shedding: Protect Goodput
entries.productionQuestion: The system can serve 10k RPS and receives 30k; what should it do?
entries.learningDelta: Beyond capacity, serving everything degrades goodput; shedding low-value work early preserves useful throughput
objectives: Distinguish throughput from goodput and explain why serving more requests can help fewer users.
Choose a queue bound and a shed trigger from the latency deadline, not from CPU alone.
Rank traffic by value and explain who gets rejected when demand exceeds capacity.
Defend the fairness and over-shedding risks of an admission policy.

entries.title: Load Testing
entries.productionQuestion: A load test passes at 10k RPS and production fails at 6k. What was unrealistic?
entries.learningDelta: Load tests must model traffic mix, data, dependencies, and open-loop arrival; a closed-loop test hides queueing and coordinated omission
objectives: Distinguish open-loop arrival from closed-loop virtual users.
Detect a test that never applied its intended load.
Explain how traffic mix and dependency latency move the capacity knee.
Design a test that finds the production knee before production does.

entries.title: Local Cache + Redis
entries.productionQuestion: Redis p99 is fine but one hot key consumes most of its capacity. Is a local cache safe?
entries.learningDelta: An in-process cache removes network hops for hot reads but introduces per-instance staleness and memory cost
objectives: Separate the latency win of a local cache from the freshness and memory costs it adds.
Read a hit-rate change together with Redis operations, staleness, and per-task memory.
Explain why a short TTL can overload Redis while a long TTL can exceed the freshness SLO.
Choose between TTL, invalidation, bypass, and task count for a hot-read path.

entries.title: Local Cache Bypass on ECS
entries.productionQuestion: A local cache speeds reads but a bad value cannot be purged. What escape hatch do you need?
entries.learningDelta: Local caches need a bypass, versioning, or kill switch so operators can recover without redeploying every task
objectives: Explain why a shared-cache flush cannot clear an in-process cache on ECS tasks.
Compare a rolling replacement, a TTL, a runtime bypass, and versioned keys by time to recover.
Design a kill switch that is fast, observable, and safe to leave in the codebase.
Choose a bypass scope that stops the bad value without overloading Redis.

entries.title: Locality-Aware Load Balancing
entries.productionQuestion: Cross-zone traffic costs rise after a mesh rollout. What policy changed?
entries.learningDelta: Locality-aware balancing prefers local endpoints but fails over when local capacity or health is insufficient
objectives: Explain how locality preference keeps traffic in a zone while endpoints are healthy.
Distinguish local capacity pressure from global capacity shortage.
Quantify the latency and cost of cross-zone spillover.
Choose between strict locality and available failover for a hot zone.

entries.title: Locks and Deadlocks
entries.productionQuestion: Writes hang and the database reports deadlocks. Which query do you inspect first?
entries.learningDelta: Lock waits and deadlocks come from transaction ordering; pg_locks and wait events reveal the blocker, but killing it has consequences
objectives: Distinguish a lock wait from a deadlock and explain why only one resolves itself.
Use a wait graph to find the blocking session rather than the waiting one.
Explain how consistent lock ordering prevents most deadlocks.
Choose between waiting, canceling a statement, and terminating a session, with the rollback cost of each.

entries.title: Log Pipeline Backpressure
entries.productionQuestion: The log agent queue is full during a traffic spike and logs are dropped. How do you protect the pipeline?
entries.learningDelta: Agents need bounded buffers and prioritization; dropping debug logs is better than blocking application threads or losing errors
objectives: Separate a local agent buffer problem from a downstream egress problem.
Choose a drop policy that preserves errors and explicitly accepts losing debug and info logs.
Explain why a disk buffer delays loss and raises log age instead of adding capacity.
Design a bounded pipeline whose failure is visible in drop and age metrics before application latency moves.

entries.title: Log Volume and Cost
entries.productionQuestion: A verbose release multiplies log volume and the ingestion budget is gone. What do you change?
entries.learningDelta: Log cost is volume × retention; level, sampling, and routing keep high-value logs while cutting noise
objectives: Compute log volume from request rate, lines per request, and retained copies.
Separate log level, sampling, routing, and retention as cost levers.
Cut spend without removing the evidence an incident needs.
Explain why a cheaper tier is not the same as a lower-volume pipeline.

entries.title: Long Transactions: Locks, Bloat, and Lag
entries.productionQuestion: A reporting query runs for 40 minutes and replication lag climbs. What is the chain?
entries.learningDelta: Long transactions hold snapshots and locks, delay vacuum, and can block replication; they turn a read into a system-wide problem
objectives: Trace how an open transaction's snapshot prevents vacuum from removing dead row versions.
Separate lock waits caused by row locks from freshness lag caused by an uncommitted write transaction.
Choose the first metric to inspect when a reporting query correlates with write timeouts and replica lag.
Bound transaction duration with timeouts and isolate reporting reads without breaking correctness.

entries.title: Lua Scripts: Atomicity and Blocking
entries.productionQuestion: A Lua script fixes a race but raises p99. What is the risk?
entries.learningDelta: Lua runs atomically on the server and blocks other commands; long scripts turn correctness fixes into latency incidents
objectives: Explain what Lua atomicity guarantees and what it does not.
Connect script duration and write rate to the shard's event-loop occupancy.
Diagnose a lost-update race and choose between Lua, a single command, and optimistic retry.
Bound a script so a correctness fix does not become a latency incident.

entries.title: Max Connections: The Limit Behind the Limit
entries.productionQuestion: The database has 500 max connections but dies at 300. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Each connection consumes memory and workers; the practical limit is lower than max_connections and depends on workload
objectives: Derive a safe connection count from memory, per-session work, and reserved slots.
Explain why the practical limit can be below max_connections.
Recognize a connection storm and the queue that forms before refusal.
Choose between raising memory, lowering sessions, and adding a pooler.

entries.title: Mesh Access Logs
entries.productionQuestion: The app has no log for a failed request. Does the mesh?
entries.learningDelta: Access logs record proxy-level status, upstream, timing, and flags; they explain failures before the app sees them
objectives: Explain why a proxy access log can contain failures the application never logged.
Read status, upstream host, duration, and response flags from one access-log line.
Choose a sampling and filtering policy that keeps error evidence.
Correlate a proxy request id with an application log when both exist.

entries.title: Mesh Circuit Breaking
entries.productionQuestion: A dependency is slow and Envoy keeps opening new connections. What limits do you set?
entries.learningDelta: Envoy circuit breakers cap connections, pending requests, and retries; they protect the upstream and fail fast locally
objectives: Calculate the concurrency a dependency needs from rate and latency.
Set connection, pending request, and retry limits that shed load locally.
Distinguish a local breaker rejection from an upstream failure.
Explain what happens when limits are raised past the upstream's capacity.

entries.title: Mesh Failover
entries.productionQuestion: A zone fails and Envoy keeps sending traffic to ejected endpoints. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Failover policy, priority groups, and health checks determine whether traffic moves; stale endpoints cause errors
objectives: Explain how Envoy priority levels decide when traffic moves to another zone.
Distinguish a capacity shortfall from traffic sent to unhealthy endpoints.
Relate health-check timing and priority configuration to failover behavior.
Design a failover test that covers detection, capacity, and return traffic.

entries.title: Mesh Retries
entries.productionQuestion: Envoy retries every 503 three times and the dependency collapses. What do you change?
entries.learningDelta: Proxy retries are powerful and dangerous; retry budgets, conditions, and per-try timeout prevent amplification
objectives: Design a retry policy from the failure condition, attempt count, and per-try deadline.
Calculate how retries change offered load against a dependency's capacity.
Use a retry budget to bound amplification and explain its user-visible cost.
Distinguish a retry that helps an isolated failure from one that sustains a shared failure.

entries.title: Mesh Timeouts
entries.productionQuestion: The proxy returns 504 before the service finishes. Which timeout won?
entries.learningDelta: Proxy timeout, route timeout, and application deadline are separate; the smallest wins and retries can stack
objectives: Identify which clock ends a request when route, per-try, and application deadlines differ.
Explain why raising the route timeout can leave a 504 unchanged.
Recognize a premature cut where the route had budget but a shorter clock fired.
Bound total user wait when retries repeat a timed-out attempt.

entries.title: Mesh Tracing
entries.productionQuestion: Traces stop at the sidecar and do not show the upstream call. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Mesh tracing requires context propagation and proxy span generation; sampling and header handling decide continuity
objectives: Distinguish a missing proxy span from a broken trace context.
Explain how injection, forwarding, and sampling change trace completeness.
Read a trace waterfall that contains application and sidecar spans.
Diagnose why an upstream call starts a new root span.

entries.title: MongoDB Replica Sets
entries.productionQuestion: The primary disappears and the app reconnects to a new node. What happened underneath?
entries.learningDelta: A replica set elects one primary; secondaries apply the oplog, and clients discover topology changes
objectives: Describe how a primary, secondaries, and the oplog keep one writable copy of the data set.
Explain why a majority of voting members is required before a new primary can accept writes.
Trace what happens to client writes during an election and after a new primary appears.
Identify stale client topology as a separate failure from the election itself.

entries.title: Mongos Routing and Targets
entries.productionQuestion: A query is slow only when it goes through mongos. What do you inspect?
entries.learningDelta: Mongos routes by shard key, merges results, and applies targeting; scatter-gather and merge overhead can dominate
objectives: Trace a query through mongos: cached metadata, shard targeting, fan-out, and result merge.
Separate router merge cost from shard execution cost using per-component signals.
Explain why a broad query can be fast on one shard and slow only through the router.
Choose a fix that reduces fan-out or merge width instead of adding shards blindly.

entries.title: Monitoring the Monitor
entries.productionQuestion: All dashboards are green and no metrics have arrived for 20 minutes. What now?
entries.learningDelta: Meta-monitoring checks scrape health, agent liveness, ingestion lag, and alert delivery; absence of data is itself an alert
objectives: Detect a telemetry outage from coverage and staleness instead of from application health.
Explain why an alert rule over an empty vector does not fire.
Set a dead man window that bounds total-outage detection time.
Design meta-monitoring that catches partial blind spots, not only total silence.

entries.title: MQTT Broker Scaling
entries.productionQuestion: You add a broker and existing clients lose their sessions. Why?
entries.learningDelta: MQTT sessions and retained state are broker-local unless clustered or bridged; scaling requires state strategy
objectives: Explain why a load balancer does not move an existing MQTT session.
Distinguish session state, subscriptions, in-flight messages, and retained state.
Compare broker-local, sticky, and shared-state cluster strategies by reconnect behavior.
Plan a broker addition that preserves sessions and retained values.

entries.title: MQTT Fan-Out
entries.productionQuestion: One telemetry topic has 50k subscribers and the broker is overloaded. How do you fan out?
entries.learningDelta: MQTT fan-out is broker-bound; shared subscriptions, topic trees, and bridging distribute subscribers across brokers
objectives: Estimate broker load from publish rate, subscriber count, and payload size.
Explain why fan-out cost grows with subscribers rather than with publishers.
Compare shared subscriptions, broker bridging, and topic-tree changes by cost and delivery semantics.
Choose a fan-out design that keeps per-subscriber delivery and broker CPU within budget.

entries.title: MQTT QoS 0, 1, and 2
entries.productionQuestion: A sensor publishes telemetry and the broker restarts. Which QoS prevents loss?
entries.learningDelta: QoS 0 is fire-and-forget, QoS 1 is at-least-once, QoS 2 is exactly-once at the protocol level with higher overhead
objectives: Map QoS 0, 1, and 2 to their delivery guarantees and packet flows.
Predict loss and duplication when a broker restarts at each QoS level.
Explain why QoS 2 is not end-to-end exactly-once for your application.
Choose a QoS level from the cost of a missing or duplicate reading.

entries.title: MQTT Retained Messages
entries.productionQuestion: A dashboard reconnects and shows no values until the next publish. What do you enable?
entries.learningDelta: Retained messages store the last value per topic and deliver it on subscribe, trading broker state for freshness
objectives: Explain how a retained message differs from a queued message.
Predict what a new subscriber sees with and without the retained flag.
Relate publish interval to dashboard staleness when no retained value exists.
State the limits of retained state across broker restarts and topic cardinality.

entries.title: mTLS in the Mesh
entries.productionQuestion: A service accepts plaintext from inside the mesh. What policy prevents it?
entries.learningDelta: mTLS authenticates both sides with certificates; permissive mode allows plaintext and hides misconfiguration
objectives: Distinguish authenticated identity from encrypted transport in a service mesh.
Explain how strict and permissive modes change what an inbound proxy accepts.
Read a mesh dashboard that looks healthy while plaintext traffic is admitted.
Choose a migration path from permissive to strict without breaking callers.

entries.title: Multi-AZ Scheduling
entries.productionQuestion: One AZ loses a node and too many tasks were packed there. How do you spread them?
entries.learningDelta: The scheduler places tasks across zones, but capacity and placement constraints can concentrate them
objectives: Predict how spread and binpack placement distribute tasks across three availability zones.
Calculate surviving capacity after one zone is lost.
Explain why a balanced pre-failure layout can still breach the desired count.
Design N+1 headroom that covers the loss of the busiest zone at peak.

entries.title: Multi-AZ vs Multi-Region
entries.productionQuestion: The business needs 99.99% and 15-minute RTO. Is Multi-AZ enough?
entries.learningDelta: Multi-AZ protects against an AZ failure with a synchronous standby; multi-region protects against a region failure with asynchronous lag and higher RTO
objectives: Distinguish the failure domain that each topology survives.
Explain why Multi-AZ has RPO 0 for an AZ failure but cannot cover a region failure.
Compare RTO and data loss across single-AZ, Multi-AZ, and multi-region.
Defend the cost of multi-region against a stated availability and RTO target.

entries.title: Multi-Region Failover
entries.productionQuestion: One region is degraded but not down. Do you fail over and risk data loss?
entries.learningDelta: Regional failover trades availability for data loss and capacity; the decision needs RPO, capacity, and a tested runbook
objectives: Compare staying in a degraded region with failing over to a standby.
Quantify data loss from replication lag before making the cutover decision.
Verify standby capacity against current demand before promoting a region.
Decide when a partial degradation does not justify a regional failover.

entries.title: N+1 Queries: Count the Round Trips
entries.productionQuestion: A page loads 200 items and makes 201 queries. Where do you fix it?
entries.learningDelta: N+1 comes from per-item queries; batching, joins, or dataloaders reduce round trips and connection pressure
objectives: Count the round trips a page makes from its item count and per-item queries.
Explain why p99 latency grows faster than the average as query count rises.
Fix N+1 with a join, an IN batch, or a dataloader and state the tradeoff of each.
Detect the pattern from query counts and connection pool pressure, not just slow query logs.

entries.title: NAT Gateway
entries.productionQuestion: Private tasks can reach S3 but not the internet. What is missing?
entries.learningDelta: NAT gateways provide outbound translation for private subnets; they are zonal, bandwidth-bound, and charge per GB
objectives: Trace private-subnet egress through a NAT gateway, its public subnet, and the internet gateway.
Explain why a NAT gateway is zonal and why a shared NAT concentrates failure across Availability Zones.
Read NAT connection pressure and port-allocation signals before users report timeouts.
Design per-AZ egress that keeps the blast radius to one Availability Zone.

entries.title: NAT Gateway Scaling
entries.productionQuestion: Egress latency rises across all private subnets and NAT is the common component. What do you check?
entries.learningDelta: NAT gateways scale per AZ and have bandwidth and port limits; one NAT for many AZs concentrates traffic and failure
objectives: Separate a NAT bandwidth limit from a per-destination port allocation limit.
Read egress latency and connection errors when the NAT is the common component.
Explain why one NAT gateway shared across Availability Zones concentrates both traffic and failure.
Design per-AZ egress that scales without turning one gateway into a single point of failure.

entries.title: Negative Caching and Bloom Filters
entries.productionQuestion: A scraper requests 10k random IDs per second. How do you protect the database?
entries.learningDelta: Negative caching stores absence with a short TTL; Bloom filters reject definitely-absent keys with a tunable false-positive rate
objectives: Size a negative cache TTL against key creation, repetition, and memory.
Explain why a Bloom filter has false positives but no false negatives for its source set.
Distinguish a false positive that adds database load from a stale marker that rejects a valid key.
Choose between an exact negative cache and a probabilistic filter for a given traffic shape.

entries.title: Network ACLs
entries.productionQuestion: Security groups allow the traffic but a subnet ACL blocks the response. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Network ACLs are stateless and evaluated per subnet; ephemeral ports must be allowed in both directions
objectives: Trace a request and its response through the inbound and outbound rules of two subnet ACLs.
Explain why a stateful security group rule does not create an ACL rule for the response.
Use ephemeral port ranges and first-match rule order to localize a one-way failure.
Tighten a broad ephemeral allow rule without closing the return path.

entries.title: Network Saturation: Bandwidth, Retransmits, and Drops
entries.productionQuestion: Throughput is below the link rate and latency climbs; what network signal do you check first?
entries.learningDelta: Bandwidth, packet loss, retransmits, and NIC queue drops are different failure modes with different fixes
objectives: Distinguish a full link from a lossy path with spare capacity.
Read retransmits, packet loss, and NIC drops as separate signals.
Explain why TCP throughput falls with loss and RTT.
Choose between more bandwidth, loss remediation, and queue tuning.

entries.title: NLB in Front of ALB: What It Buys and Costs
entries.productionQuestion: You need static IPs and ALB path routing at very high connection counts. How do you combine them?
entries.learningDelta: An NLB can front ALBs with static IPs and high connection capacity, adding a hop and changing source-IP and TLS behavior
objectives: Explain what an NLB adds in front of an ALB and what it cannot add.
Trace TLS termination, client IP, and health checks across the two layers.
Predict the latency and failure behavior of the extra hop.
Decide between NLB fronting, DNS sharding, and a single ALB.

entries.title: Noisy Neighbor
entries.productionQuestion: One tenant's batch workload doubles the latency of everyone else. What do you do?
entries.learningDelta: Noisy neighbors need per-tenant quotas, isolation, or scheduling; shared pools maximize utilization and risk
objectives: Explain how one tenant's CPU demand reaches another tenant's latency in a shared pool.
Distinguish a quota, a reserved capacity share, and separate pools as isolation mechanisms.
Diagnose the noisy neighbor from per-tenant latency and shared-pool saturation.
Choose an isolation level and defend its utilization cost.

entries.title: Object-Storage Streaming Latency
entries.productionQuestion: Object storage delivers high throughput but p99 reads are slow. Which workload is affected?
entries.learningDelta: Object storage favors throughput and durability; per-request latency and metadata operations make it unsuitable for some low-latency paths
objectives: Read a latency histogram instead of a single average or throughput number.
Identify which workloads a high-throughput, high-p99 storage path actually breaks.
Estimate how object size, cache hit rate, and concurrency move p50 and p99 differently.
Choose a mitigation that preserves durability while meeting a latency budget.

entries.title: Observability Cost per Request
entries.productionQuestion: Observability is 25% of infrastructure cost and growing faster than traffic. Where do you cut?
entries.learningDelta: Telemetry has volume, cardinality, and retention costs; sampling and tiering should follow incident value, not default retention
objectives: Break telemetry spend into volume, cardinality, and retention components.
Identify which component is driving cost per request while traffic is flat.
Choose a cut that preserves the signals used in incidents.
Defend the coverage cost of each sampling or retention decision.

entries.title: On-Call Handoff
entries.productionQuestion: A new shift starts and immediately asks what changed. What belongs in the handoff?
entries.learningDelta: A handoff covers active incidents, recent changes, risky deploys, expiring certificates, and known gaps
objectives: Name the five kinds of context a shift handoff must transfer.
Explain why an unowned risk survives a handoff that lists it.
Distinguish a status summary from an operational handoff.
Design a handoff that makes the next action and owner explicit.

entries.title: One Dashboard, One Decision
entries.productionQuestion: It is 3 a.m. and the dashboard has every metric but no next step. How do you redesign it?
entries.learningDelta: A useful dashboard orders signals by the decision they support and links the next check, not every available metric
objectives: Trace a slow incident decision to panel count, relevance, ordering, and missing links.
Design a dashboard around one decision and its next check.
Distinguish context panels from decision panels.
Measure dashboard quality by time-to-decision rather than panel coverage.

entries.title: OOM Kills
entries.productionQuestion: A task restarts with exit code 137. Was it CPU throttling or memory?
entries.learningDelta: Exit 137 is SIGKILL; OOM kills leave a stop reason and memory metrics, while CPU throttling does not kill
objectives: Separate an OOM kill from CPU throttling using exit code, stop reason, and the memory curve.
Calculate how long a memory trend has before it reaches the task limit.
Fix the workload or the limit without hiding the trend behind restarts.

entries.title: OpenTelemetry Context Propagation
entries.productionQuestion: The trace stops at the queue consumer and shows two unrelated traces. What broke?
entries.learningDelta: Trace context must be injected and extracted across every hop, including queues and background jobs
objectives: Read a traceparent header and name the trace and parent span it carries.
Find the hop where context is lost by comparing root spans with the expected request path.
Carry context across a queue message and a background job without starting a new root.
Separate trace continuity from baggage, which travels with the request but does not join spans.

entries.title: Origin Shield and Request Collapsing
entries.productionQuestion: A popular object expires and every edge requests it from the origin. How do you collapse the misses?
entries.learningDelta: Origin shield centralizes misses and request collapsing turns concurrent misses into one origin fetch
objectives: Explain how simultaneous edge expiries become an origin request storm.
Distinguish per-edge request collapsing from a shared origin shield.
Measure origin burst, origin request rate, and the latency cost of an extra cache tier.
Choose a collapsing design that protects the origin without making the shield a new bottleneck.

entries.title: Outlier Detection
entries.productionQuestion: One pod returns errors and Envoy ejects healthy pods too. What threshold is wrong?
entries.learningDelta: Outlier detection ejects hosts based on consecutive errors and ejection percentage; overly aggressive settings remove capacity
objectives: Explain how passive outlier detection decides that a host is bad.
Predict how consecutive errors and max ejection percentage change capacity.
Recognize a death spiral where ejection removes healthy capacity.
Recover a cluster without disabling detection entirely.

entries.title: Paging Fatigue
entries.productionQuestion: On-call receives 80 pages a week and misses the real one. What do you measure?
entries.learningDelta: Page load must be actionable and bounded; measure pages per shift and the fraction that lead to action, not raw alert count
objectives: Measure page load per shift instead of counting raw alerts.
Distinguish actionable pages from noise and from missed detection.
Explain why a larger rotation redistributes fatigue but does not remove it.
Design a paging change that lowers volume without lowering detection.

entries.title: Parameter Groups: Change With a Plan
entries.productionQuestion: A parameter change improves one query and breaks another. How do you roll it out?
entries.learningDelta: Parameter groups apply engine settings; some are dynamic, some require reboot, and cluster-level settings have different scope
objectives: Classify a setting as dynamic or static and name its apply path.
Explain cluster-level versus instance-level parameter scope.
Plan a change with a canary, a maintenance window, and a rollback.
Predict the blast radius of a reboot during peak traffic.

entries.title: Partition Count: More Is Not Free
entries.productionQuestion: The topic has 200 partitions and failover takes minutes. What did the partition count cost?
entries.learningDelta: More partitions add parallelism but increase metadata, rebalance time, file handles, and end-to-end latency
objectives: Size a partition count from throughput, consumer parallelism, and headroom.
Explain how partition count raises metadata, rebalance, and file-handle cost.
Diagnose slow controller failover and rebalance from partition count.
Choose a partition count with a tested failover and rollback plan.

entries.title: Partitioning and Sharding
entries.productionQuestion: A table is too large for one writer. Do you partition, shard, or archive?
entries.learningDelta: Partitioning splits one logical table for maintenance; sharding splits writers across nodes and adds routing and cross-shard complexity
objectives: Separate the maintenance benefit of partitioning from the write-capacity benefit of sharding.
Predict when a hot shard or cross-shard query dominates latency after a split.
Choose between partitioning, sharding, and archiving for a stated growth and traffic shape.
Name the routing, rebalancing, and query constraints a shard key imposes.

entries.title: Password Hashing: Cost, Salt, and Timing
entries.productionQuestion: A leaked database contains unsalted SHA-256 hashes; what did the team get wrong?
entries.learningDelta: Password hashing uses a unique salt and a tunable work factor (bcrypt/Argon2); fast general-purpose hashes are the wrong tool
objectives: Explain why fast hashes such as SHA-256 are unsuitable for password storage.
Choose a salt and work factor that make offline cracking expensive without breaking login latency.
Avoid timing and error-message leaks in the login path.
Plan a migration from a weak hash without invalidating every stored credential.

entries.title: PCI DSS Scope Reduction
entries.productionQuestion: The card-data environment includes the whole platform. How do you reduce scope?
entries.learningDelta: PCI scope follows cardholder data and connected systems; tokenization and segmentation shrink the audit boundary
objectives: Identify which systems store, process, transmit, or connect to cardholder data.
Explain how tokenization removes primary account numbers from downstream systems.
Evaluate segmentation as an enforced boundary rather than a diagram.
Choose scope reductions and state their operational tradeoffs.

entries.title: Peak Event Planning
entries.productionQuestion: A marketing event will send 10× traffic in two weeks. What do you do now?
entries.learningDelta: Peak planning works backward from the event: forecast, load test, pre-scale, freeze changes, and staff the response
objectives: Work backward from an event date to the capacity and test milestones.
Decide when pre-scaling is required instead of reactive scaling.
Explain why a partial load test does not certify event capacity.
Sequence the freeze, rollback, and staffing decisions around the event.

entries.title: Percentiles: What the Average Hides
entries.productionQuestion: Mean latency is 80ms and p99 is 1.9s; which number describes the user experience?
entries.learningDelta: Averages hide tail pain; p99 and p999 describe the slow requests that drive timeouts and retries
objectives: Read a latency distribution instead of a single average.
Choose a percentile based on the user action and the traffic volume.
Explain why a small slow cohort can dominate timeouts and retries.
Avoid averaging percentiles across instances or time windows.

entries.title: PgBouncer: Pool Before the Database
entries.productionQuestion: 200 app tasks each open 20 connections and the database refuses new ones. How do you pool?
entries.learningDelta: PgBouncer multiplexes client connections onto fewer server connections; transaction pooling breaks session-level features
objectives: Size a PgBouncer pool from client concurrency and the database connection limit.
Distinguish session pooling from transaction pooling and name what transaction pooling breaks.
Diagnose session-state failures that appear only after transaction pooling is enabled.
Decide when to change the application instead of increasing the pool size.

entries.title: PHI Handling
entries.productionQuestion: A log contains a diagnosis code and a patient identifier. Is that PHI?
entries.learningDelta: PHI is health information tied to an individual; identifiers plus health data create obligations across logs, backups, and vendors
objectives: Decide whether a field combination is PHI from the data, not from the system that stores it.
Trace how PHI is copied into logs, analytics stores, and vendor exports.
Distinguish validated de-identification from hashing, masking, or tokenization.
Contain PHI that has reached an unapproved system and verify the fix.

entries.title: PII Redaction in Telemetry
entries.productionQuestion: A debug log contains an email and a token. What is your containment plan?
entries.learningDelta: Redaction must happen at emit time and be verified; logs and traces are copies of production data with different retention
objectives: Trace how a sensitive field travels from a debug statement into retained telemetry.
Choose an emit-time control that survives new fields and new services.
Size the blast radius from leak rate, retention, and copy count.
Run a containment sequence for a credential or personal data leak.

entries.title: Playbooks vs Runbooks
entries.productionQuestion: A novel incident has no runbook. What playbook applies?
entries.learningDelta: Runbooks handle known alerts; playbooks give decision frameworks for unknown failures
objectives: Distinguish a runbook for a known alert from a playbook for an unknown failure.
Apply a decision framework that bounds scope before committing to a cause.
Recognize how a playbook becomes a rigid script and misses context.
Choose the next discriminating test instead of the most familiar one.

entries.title: Poison Messages
entries.productionQuestion: One malformed event fails every retry and the partition stops. How do you recover?
entries.learningDelta: A poison message blocks in-order processing; validation, retry limits, and DLQs isolate it without losing the stream
objectives: Recognize head-of-line blocking from a single failing record.
Explain why unbounded retries turn one bad record into a stalled partition.
Choose a retry budget and quarantine path that keeps the partition moving.
Decide what validation belongs at the producer, the consumer, or both.

entries.title: Policy as Code
entries.productionQuestion: A production bucket is public despite a policy saying it must not be. How do you prevent it?
entries.learningDelta: Policy as code evaluates infrastructure before deploy and continuously detects drift; prevention is cheaper than audit findings
objectives: Turn a written control into an executable policy with an owner and a test.
Place policy gates in the deploy path so a noncompliant resource cannot reach production.
Detect drift and out-of-band changes that never pass through the pipeline.
Manage exceptions and emergency changes without silently disabling the control.

entries.title: Policy Conflicts
entries.productionQuestion: Two policies set different timeouts for the same service. Which one applies?
entries.learningDelta: Mesh policy precedence depends on scope and specificity; conflicting policies are hard to debug without a clear ownership model
objectives: Explain how Kuma selects one policy when several match a proxy.
Distinguish an intended policy from the effective configuration.
Predict the effect of a selector that matches only part of a workload.
