Design policy ownership that keeps overlapping scopes debuggable.

entries.title: Postmortem Action Quality
entries.productionQuestion: The action is “be more careful” and the incident recurs. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Good actions change systems, have verification, and address contributing factors; human vigilance is not a control
objectives: Rewrite vigilance advice as a change to a system condition.
Attach a verification that would fail if the condition returned.
Cover the contributing factors rather than the most visible symptom.
Explain why unverified actions produce recurrence even when they ship.

entries.title: Private Hosted Zones
entries.productionQuestion: An internal service name resolves publicly. What is wrong?
entries.learningDelta: Private hosted zones are associated with VPCs and only resolve there; public zones resolve globally
objectives: Explain why a private hosted zone answers only for associated VPCs and inbound Resolver paths.
Distinguish a missing association from a missing record and from a public-zone copy.
Recognize split-horizon DNS and decide when a public record for the same name is intentional.
Predict which zone answers a query from the internet, an associated VPC, and an unassociated VPC.

entries.title: PrivateLink
entries.productionQuestion: A SaaS provider needs to reach your VPC without overlapping CIDRs. What do you use?
entries.learningDelta: PrivateLink exposes a service through an endpoint in the consumer VPC, avoiding CIDR overlap and broad routing
objectives: Describe how an interface endpoint, an endpoint service, and a Network Load Balancer form a PrivateLink path.
Choose endpoint Availability Zone coverage that does not depend on a single zone.
Separate endpoint acceptance, endpoint policy, and provider target health when connectivity fails.
Decide when PrivateLink is a better fit than VPC peering or a transit gateway.

entries.title: Probabilistic Early Expiration
entries.productionQuestion: A hot key expires in sync across all app instances. How do you refresh early?
entries.learningDelta: Probabilistic early expiration spreads refreshes before TTL expiry, reducing synchronized misses at the cost of extra recomputation
objectives: Explain how XFetch turns a TTL edge into a probability that rises near expiry.
Relate beta and recompute time to the early-refresh window and the extra recomputation it causes.
Choose beta from a backend capacity and freshness budget rather than from a default.
Recognize when early expiration cannot replace TTL jitter or request coalescing.

entries.title: Producer Acks
entries.productionQuestion: A producer returns success and the broker loses the event. What acks setting was used?
entries.learningDelta: acks=0/1/all trade latency for durability; acks=all with min.insync.replicas is required for strong guarantees
objectives: Explain what acks=0, acks=1, and acks=all wait for before returning success.
Relate min.insync.replicas to the in-sync replica set and write availability.
Diagnose acknowledged data loss from leader failure and replication settings.
Choose an acks and min.insync.replicas pair for a stated durability target.

entries.title: PromQL Rate: Windows, Resets, and Aliasing
entries.productionQuestion: Your rate query shows spikes every minute that do not match user impact. Why?
entries.learningDelta: rate() extrapolates over a window; the window must cover several scrapes and align with the counter's reset behavior
objectives: Choose a rate window that covers enough scrapes for a stable result.
Explain how a short window aliases a burst into an invented spike.
Distinguish rate() from irate() by smoothing and reset behavior.
Read an extrapolation factor and decide when a panel is under-sampled.

entries.title: Query Plans: Why the Index Is Ignored
entries.productionQuestion: An index exists but the planner chooses a sequential scan. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Plans depend on statistics, selectivity, cost, and predicates; stale stats or functions on columns defeat indexes
objectives: Read estimated rows, actual rows, and loop counts in EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
Explain how stale statistics make a nested loop look cheap to the planner.
Distinguish a plan that is wrong because of cost estimates from one that cannot use an index.
Refresh statistics or rewrite a predicate without guessing at planner internals.

entries.title: Queue Depth vs Latency
entries.productionQuestion: Queue depth is 10k but latency is fine; another queue has depth 100 and is timing out. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Queue depth alone is ambiguous; arrival rate, service rate, and age of oldest message determine user impact
objectives: Explain why queue depth is not a latency signal by itself.
Use oldest message age and service rate to estimate wait.
Compare two queues with different depths and different drain rates.
Choose the backlog metric that matches the user-facing latency budget.

entries.title: Queueing Headroom
entries.productionQuestion: The fleet runs at 85% CPU and p99 is unstable. What utilization target should you set?
entries.learningDelta: Latency rises nonlinearly near saturation; the safe target depends on variability and failure headroom, not a universal percentage
objectives: Relate a utilization target to the latency budget it leaves at the queue.
Explain why the same 85% target is safe for calm traffic and unsafe for bursty traffic.
Reserve headroom for a zone failure before choosing the target.
Defend the cost of headroom against the cost of an SLO breach.

entries.title: Rate Limiting: Token Bucket vs Fixed Window
entries.productionQuestion: A fixed-window limiter allows 2× the intended rate at the window boundary; how do you fix it?
entries.learningDelta: Token bucket smooths average rate while allowing a bounded burst; fixed windows permit boundary spikes
objectives: Explain how a fixed window can admit twice its configured rate across a boundary.
Choose between token bucket, fixed window, and sliding window for a traffic shape.
Read admitted, rejected, and burst-multiplier signals together.
Defend a burst allowance without turning it into an unbounded exception.

entries.title: RDS and Aurora Architecture
entries.productionQuestion: A read query is hitting the writer and piling up locks. Which endpoint and topology should it use?
entries.learningDelta: RDS and Aurora separate compute from storage differently; endpoints and replicas determine where reads and writes go
objectives: Trace a read and a write from the application endpoint to the instance that serves it.
Choose the writer, reader, or instance endpoint for a workload and explain the consequence.
Compare how RDS and Aurora place storage and replicas, and what each replica can serve.
Recognize reads routed to the writer as a capacity and contention problem.

entries.title: RDS Proxy: Managed Pooling and Failover
entries.productionQuestion: A database failover causes a connection storm and a long outage. How does RDS Proxy change it?
entries.learningDelta: RDS Proxy pools and holds connections, masking failover from clients, but adds a hop and has its own limits
objectives: Explain how RDS Proxy keeps idle application connections during a database failover.
Distinguish the client connection population from the database connection pool.
Size the proxy pool so the new writer is not overwhelmed after failover.
Name when a proxy makes an outage worse: too large a pool, pinning, and borrow timeouts.

entries.title: Reachability Analyzer
entries.productionQuestion: You need to know whether a new route will work. Can you test without sending traffic?
entries.learningDelta: Reachability Analyzer evaluates configuration paths and returns the blocking component; it does not prove live traffic behavior
objectives: Read a Reachability Analyzer result as a configuration path, not a live traffic test.
Identify the blocking component by evaluation order: route, network ACL, security group.
Distinguish an unreachable configuration from a reachable configuration with a failing application.
Use the analyzer before a production change and know what still needs a packet test.

entries.title: Read Concern
entries.productionQuestion: A read returns data that is later rolled back. Which read concern was used?
entries.learningDelta: Read concern controls the visibility and durability of reads; local can return data not yet majority-committed
objectives: Distinguish local, majority, linearizable, and snapshot read concern by what they guarantee.
Explain how a local read can return a write that is later rolled back after a primary crash.
Choose a read concern from the consistency and latency the product needs.
Use causal sessions and maxTimeMS with the read concern that requires them.

entries.title: Read Preference
entries.productionQuestion: A dashboard reads from a lagging secondary and shows old data. Which read preference fits?
entries.learningDelta: Read preference trades freshness for locality and load; primary, primaryPreferred, secondary, and nearest have different failure behavior
objectives: Choose a read preference mode from the product's freshness and availability requirements.
Explain how secondary reads become stale and how `maxStalenessSeconds` filters candidates.
Distinguish primaryPreferred from secondaryPreferred when the primary fails.
Recognize that nearest is a latency choice, not a freshness guarantee.

entries.title: Read Replica Routing Without Stale Reads
entries.productionQuestion: A user updates a profile and immediately reads an old value from a replica. How do you route?
entries.learningDelta: Read routing must respect read-your-writes; sticky-to-primary windows, session consistency, or write-through caches solve different cases
objectives: Route reads by consistency requirement instead of one global read/write split.
Design a read-your-writes rule using a post-write primary window or a version boundary.
Quantify the writer capacity cost of stickiness and the staleness cost of replica reads.
Choose between sticky sessions, version tokens, and write-through caches for different read paths.

entries.title: Read Replicas: Offload Without Staleness Surprises
entries.productionQuestion: Read replicas cut Redis CPU but users see stale data. What is the tradeoff?
entries.learningDelta: Replicas offload reads but replicate asynchronously; lag creates staleness, and hot-key reads can saturate a replica instead
objectives: Separate primary CPU relief from the freshness cost of replica reads.
Quantify staleness from replication lag and the share of reads routed to replicas.
Explain why adding replicas can move the bottleneck instead of removing it.
Choose read routing and a failover plan that match the freshness budget.

entries.title: Read-After-Write Consistency
entries.productionQuestion: A user saves a setting and the next page load shows the old value. How do you fix it without going back to the primary for everything?
entries.learningDelta: Read-after-write requires routing the user's reads to a consistent source for a window, or propagating a version token
objectives: Separate a stale read from a lost write by checking the primary and the replica replay position.
Choose between a sticky primary window, a version token, and primary-only reads for a read path.
Size the consistency policy so only reads that need freshness pay for it.
Explain how a cache adds a second staleness boundary after the replica catches up.

entries.title: Rebalancing: Stop the World
entries.productionQuestion: Adding one consumer pauses the whole group for 40 seconds. What causes the pause?
entries.learningDelta: Rebalances revoke and reassign partitions; eager protocols pause all consumers, cooperative protocols reduce the blast radius
objectives: Trace a rebalance from a membership change through partition revocation and reassignment.
Compare eager and cooperative protocols by which consumers stop processing and for how long.
Relate pause length to group size, partition count, and the session or poll timeout.
Choose a scaling and protocol change that keeps consumer lag inside its freshness budget.

entries.title: Reconstructing the Incident Timeline
entries.productionQuestion: The postmortem says the rollback started at 14:20 but the graphs disagree. Which clock do you trust?
entries.learningDelta: Timelines require synchronized timestamps, deploy markers, and event sources; clock skew and missing annotations create false causality
objectives: Reconstruct event order from metrics, logs, deploy markers, and human decisions.
Detect when clock skew reverses cause and effect.
Choose which clock to trust and how to state uncertainty in a timeline.
Add annotations and synchronization checks that make the next timeline defensible.

entries.title: Redis Cluster Failover
entries.productionQuestion: A primary fails over and clients see a burst of errors. What does the cluster guarantee?
entries.learningDelta: Redis Cluster promotes a replica after failure detection; clients must refresh topology, retry safely, and tolerate a short write outage
objectives: Trace failure detection, election, and replica promotion in a Redis Cluster shard.
Separate the cluster's availability guarantee from the client's stale-topology behavior.
Explain when a failover can lose acknowledged writes and when a partition is worse.
Design a bounded retry and topology-refresh policy that recovers without a write storm.

entries.title: Redis Cluster Resharding: MOVED and ASK
entries.productionQuestion: During a reshard, some clients receive MOVED and others time out. What is happening?
entries.learningDelta: Redis Cluster redirects keys with MOVED and ASK during migration; clients must follow redirects and handle transient failures
objectives: Explain when Redis Cluster returns MOVED and when it returns ASK.
Trace a client request through a slot migration from source to target.
Predict which clients fail when redirect support is incomplete.
Plan a reshard that bounds migration load and keeps clients correct.

entries.title: Redis Connection Pool Exhaustion
entries.productionQuestion: Services time out waiting for a Redis connection while Redis CPU is low. What is the bottleneck?
entries.learningDelta: Pool exhaustion is a local queueing problem; too few connections wait, too many multiply sessions and failover churn
objectives: Use arrival rate and service time to calculate the concurrency a pool must cover.
Distinguish pool wait from Redis latency using Redis CPU, pool wait, and queue depth together.
Size a pool without exceeding the fleet's Redis connection budget.
Explain why a large pool makes failover and reconnect storms worse.

entries.title: Redis Data Types and Their Cost
entries.productionQuestion: A leaderboard rewrite lowers latency but memory triples. Which data type caused it?
entries.learningDelta: Data type choice sets memory overhead, operation complexity, and atomicity; the wrong type makes a fast operation expensive at scale
objectives: Explain how a key's encoding changes memory per member and read cost.
Tell a latency win from a memory cost when the payload is the same.
Estimate whether a sorted set fits a fixed shard memory budget.
Choose a structure by its operations, not by one benchmark.

entries.title: Redis Memory Fragmentation
entries.productionQuestion: Redis used_memory is 6GB but the process uses 10GB and the host is OOMing. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Allocator fragmentation, peak memory, and replica buffers make RSS larger than the logical dataset; fragmentation ratio explains the gap
objectives: Distinguish used_memory from resident set size and explain the gap.
Read fragmentation ratio alongside workload churn and replica buffers.
Size a container for peak RSS rather than the current logical dataset.
Choose between defragmentation, buffer limits, and more headroom.

entries.title: Redis Persistence: RDB, AOF, and Loss Windows
entries.productionQuestion: Redis restarts and 40 seconds of writes are gone. Which persistence setting was used?
entries.learningDelta: RDB snapshots lose writes between snapshots; AOF reduces the loss window at fsync cost; caching may not need either
objectives: Quantify the loss window of RDB, AOF everysec, AOF always, and no persistence.
Separate durability from restart time when choosing a mode.
Explain why the default AOF policy still permits a small write loss.
Choose persistence from the data's value, not from the Redis default.

entries.title: Redis vs Memcached
entries.productionQuestion: You need sorted sets, persistence, and pub/sub. Is Memcached simpler and faster enough?
entries.learningDelta: Memcached is a simple multithreaded cache; Redis adds data structures, persistence, replication, and cluster semantics at operational cost
objectives: Compare Redis and Memcached by required primitives, not by a generic benchmark.
Explain how the threading model changes the capacity story.
Recognize when a missing primitive forces a second system or a database fallback.
Justify the operational cost of the richer engine for a specific workload.

entries.title: Replication Lag and the Oplog
entries.productionQuestion: Replica lag grows during a write burst and then the secondary falls off the oplog. What happens?
entries.learningDelta: Secondaries apply the capped oplog; if they fall behind the window they need a full resync, not a quick catch-up
objectives: Relate write rate, oplog size, and entry size to the oplog window.
Distinguish a secondary that is merely behind from one that has fallen off the oplog.
Explain why falling off the oplog requires a full resync instead of incremental catch-up.
Choose between reducing write load, increasing apply capacity, and enlarging the oplog.

entries.title: Replication Lag: Measure It Before You Trust It
entries.productionQuestion: The replica is healthy but users see stale data. Which lag metric do you trust?
entries.learningDelta: Replication lag is both time and byte based; a replica can be current in bytes yet slow to apply, and vice versa
objectives: Compare time-based lag with byte-based lag and explain when each hides a backlog.
Distinguish WAL that has not arrived from WAL that has arrived but not been replayed.
Estimate stale reads from the replay backlog and the read freshness target.
Choose the metric that matches the failure: transfer, replay, or recent-transaction delay.

entries.title: Replication Thread Bottlenecks
entries.productionQuestion: Replica CPU is low but lag grows during a write burst. Which resource is the bottleneck?
entries.learningDelta: Replication apply is often single-threaded or limited by I/O; more replicas do not fix a slow apply path
objectives: Explain why apply lag grows while replica CPU is low.
Distinguish apply capacity from network and CPU capacity.
Predict lag growth from write rate and apply throughput.
Choose a fix that raises apply throughput instead of adding replicas.

entries.title: Request Coalescing: One Miss, One Fetch
entries.productionQuestion: Fifty requests miss the same key at once. How many database queries should run?
entries.learningDelta: Single-flight coalescing lets one request compute while others wait or receive stale data; it trades latency for backend protection
objectives: Distinguish a concurrent miss storm from a general traffic increase.
Explain how per-instance single-flight bounds backend work at one fetch per key in flight.
Choose between making waiters block and serving stale data while a refresh runs.
Design error, timeout, and fallback behavior for a coalesced fetch.

entries.title: Reserved Instances
entries.productionQuestion: RI coverage is 80% but the bill still rises. What changed?
entries.learningDelta: RIs discount steady-state usage but are tied to instance family, region, and term; workload drift wastes coverage
objectives: Distinguish Reserved Instance coverage from utilization.
Explain which attributes a reservation must match to apply.
Diagnose a bill increase when headline coverage looks healthy.
Choose between modifying, exchanging, or re-buying coverage as the fleet changes.

entries.title: Resource Access Manager
entries.productionQuestion: You need one Transit Gateway for four accounts. How do you share it?
entries.learningDelta: RAM shares supported resources; consumers attach but ownership, quotas, and route policy stay with the owner
objectives: Create a resource share for a transit gateway and distinguish the owner's controls from the participant's.
Explain why a participant VPC attachment can be created but remain unusable.
Diagnose an attachment that is rejected because the gateway's attachment capacity is exhausted.
Recognize the difference between an over-broad share and an attachment that never completes.

entries.title: Retention and Downsampling Tradeoffs
entries.productionQuestion: Compliance needs one year, dashboards need 30 days, and disk is full. What do you keep?
entries.learningDelta: Retention tiers and downsampling preserve long-range trends while reducing resolution and cost
objectives: Separate the audit retention requirement from the dashboard retention requirement.
Estimate disk from series count, sample interval, and retention tiers.
Explain what downsampling preserves and what it loses.
Design a retention policy that keeps required evidence and fits the disk budget.

entries.title: Retention and Legal Hold
entries.productionQuestion: A legal hold arrives while the retention job is deleting records. What do you do?
entries.learningDelta: Retention schedules must be enforceable and suspendable; legal hold overrides deletion and requires evidence of preservation
objectives: Separate a retention schedule from a legal hold and explain how they interact.
Trace a hold to every copy, index, cache, and backup that must preserve data.
Design deletion that is enforceable, observable, and suspendable.
Produce evidence that preserved records were not altered or deleted.

entries.title: Retention and Replay
entries.productionQuestion: A consumer is down for two days and retention is 24 hours. What happens?
entries.learningDelta: Retention bounds replay; time and size limits delete segments, and a consumer beyond the window loses data
objectives: Explain how time and size retention delete whole log segments rather than individual records.
Estimate the replay window from retention, segment size, and produce rate.
Recognize when a consumer's committed offset is older than the earliest retained offset.
Choose retention and replay capacity from a recovery-time objective and a storage budget.

entries.title: Retries, Backoff, and Jitter
entries.productionQuestion: A dependency returns 503 for two seconds; why did traffic triple?
entries.learningDelta: Synchronized retries amplify failure; exponential backoff with jitter spreads retries and caps amplification
objectives: Calculate retry amplification from attempts, failure rate, and a retry budget.
Explain why synchronized retries keep a dependency down after the trigger clears.
Choose a backoff, jitter, and budget combination that recovers inside the SLO.
Distinguish a retry policy problem from a dependency capacity problem.

entries.title: Retry Storms in Production
entries.productionQuestion: A dependency blips and the whole platform melts down for 20 minutes. What is the first move?
entries.learningDelta: In a retry storm, reduce retries and load before tuning the dependency; retry budgets and breakers stop the feedback loop
objectives: Diagnose amplification by comparing dependency load with original request rate.
Stop a retry storm with a budget or breaker before attempting a dependency fix.
Explain why a dependency can stay down after the original fault clears.
Order the recovery actions so the backlog does not restart the storm.

entries.title: Retryable Writes
entries.productionQuestion: A write fails during failover and the driver retries it. Could it apply twice?
entries.learningDelta: Retryable writes use a session and transaction number so the server can deduplicate retries within a window
objectives: Explain how the driver and server use a session and transaction number for a retry.
Separate a transient network error from an ambiguous write result.
Identify when a retry can still duplicate an effect or fail outright.
Decide where retry belongs: driver, application, or an idempotent operation.

entries.title: Right to Erasure
entries.productionQuestion: A deletion request completes in the database but the data remains in logs and backups. What now?
entries.learningDelta: Erasure requires discovery and deletion or irreversible anonymization across primary data, derived data, logs, and backup policy
objectives: Choose between deletion, irreversible anonymization, and suppression for each class of store.
Trace a deletion request through primary data, derived data, logs, and backups.
Design a backup policy that prevents a restore from resurrecting an erased record.
Prove completion with per-system evidence instead of a single database row count.

entries.title: Rightsizing
entries.productionQuestion: Half the fleet runs at 15% CPU and the bill is high. Why not downsize everything?
entries.learningDelta: Rightsizing uses utilization, memory, and burst behavior; averages hide peaks, and downsizing can break latency SLOs
objectives: Separate average utilization from the peak that sets latency.
Identify when memory, not CPU, blocks a smaller instance size.
Choose a rightsizing change that keeps p99 inside the SLO.
Explain the cost and risk of sizing for the peak instead of the average.

entries.title: Rollback Data Loss
entries.productionQuestion: A rollback restores the old code but the new code sent emails. What is irreversible?
entries.learningDelta: Rollback restores software, not external side effects; migrations, messages, and third-party calls need compensating actions
objectives: Separate reversible software state from irreversible external effects.
Identify writes, messages, and third-party calls that a rollback cannot undo.
Design compensating actions for effects that already left the system.
Bound the rollback window with drain, idempotency, and reconciliation.

entries.title: Rollback vs Roll-Forward
entries.productionQuestion: A bad release is live and the database has new rows. Do you roll back or fix forward?
entries.learningDelta: Rollback restores known code but may be incompatible with new data; roll-forward is faster only when the fix is understood and tested
objectives: Compare rollback and roll-forward on code, data, and fix readiness.
Explain why new-format rows can make a code rollback unsafe.
Decide when an untested fix makes roll-forward the riskier path.
Plan a safe path when neither option is clean.

entries.title: Rolling Deployments
entries.productionQuestion: A rolling deploy causes a brief 503 spike. What is the capacity math?
entries.learningDelta: Rolling deploys trade capacity for speed; minimum healthy and maximum surge determine whether the fleet survives the transition
objectives: Calculate the capacity floor a rolling deployment is allowed to reach.
Distinguish the minimum healthy floor from the maximum surge allowance.
Explain why zero surge with a 100 percent healthy minimum cannot make progress.
Choose rolling settings that keep available capacity above the request rate.

entries.title: Route 53 Health Checks
entries.productionQuestion: Route 53 still sends traffic to a dead region. What does its health check actually observe?
entries.learningDelta: Route 53 health checks probe endpoints from multiple locations and can be calculated or CloudWatch-backed; thresholds determine failover speed
objectives: Explain what a Route 53 endpoint health check observes and what it cannot see.
Choose an interval and failure threshold that meet a failover objective without flapping.
Use calculated and CloudWatch-backed checks when a direct endpoint probe is the wrong signal.
Diagnose a green health check while the user request path is failing.

entries.title: Route 53 Resolver
entries.productionQuestion: An on-premises service cannot resolve a private hosted zone. What do you configure?
entries.learningDelta: Resolver endpoints forward DNS between VPCs and on-premises; inbound and outbound endpoints serve different directions
objectives: Choose an inbound or outbound Resolver endpoint from the direction of the DNS query.
Trace a hybrid query from the on-premises resolver to the private hosted zone and back.
Detect a forwarding loop and distinguish it from a missing rule or a missing zone association.
Size Resolver endpoint IPs against the documented per-IP query limit and add interfaces before saturation.

entries.title: Route 53 Routing Policies
entries.productionQuestion: You need gradual regional migration with fast rollback. Which routing policy fits?
entries.learningDelta: Weighted routing shifts traffic gradually; failover is binary; latency optimizes user location; geolocation enforces locality
objectives: Compare failover, weighted, latency, geolocation, and multivalue routing for a migration.
Explain why a policy can be healthy but unable to express the desired traffic split.
Design a gradual migration and rollback that accounts for DNS TTL and new-region capacity.

entries.title: Route Propagation
entries.productionQuestion: Two attachments advertise the same prefix. Which path does traffic take?
entries.learningDelta: Longest prefix wins; for equal prefixes, route origin and propagation rules decide, and asymmetric paths are common
objectives: Apply longest-prefix match before comparing route type or BGP attributes.
Order a static route, a VPC-propagated route, and a VPN-propagated route for the same prefix.
Explain how AS path length breaks a tie between routes from the same attachment type.
Recognize an asymmetric return path and choose between route symmetry and inspection.

entries.title: Route Table Blackholes
entries.productionQuestion: The instance has a route to the destination but packets disappear. What does the route target do?
entries.learningDelta: A route can point to a blackhole or an attachment that is unavailable; route presence does not guarantee forwarding
objectives: Read a route table by destination, target, and state instead of assuming a matching route forwards traffic.
Distinguish a blackhole target from a missing route, a saturated target, and a missing return path.
Use route state, target attachment state, and both-direction checks to localize a silent drop.
Decide when to restore a target, replace a route, or add capacity without widening the blast radius.

entries.title: RUM and Core Web Vitals
entries.productionQuestion: Server p95 is 200ms but mobile users see a 4s LCP. Where do you look?
entries.learningDelta: RUM captures real device, network, and rendering performance; field percentiles differ from lab and server metrics
objectives: Separate server response time from the browser experience a user actually has.
Read LCP, CLS, and INP as field metrics with percentile budgets.
Explain why a p75 can miss while an average or a server metric passes.
Prioritize a frontend fix using device, network, and third-party evidence.

entries.title: Runbooks
entries.productionQuestion: The same alert is handled differently by each engineer. What do you standardize?
entries.learningDelta: A runbook gives ordered checks, expected signals, safe actions, and escalation points for one alert
objectives: Identify the five parts of a runbook that make it safe to execute under pressure.
Explain why an untested topology assumption turns a routine step into a harmful action.
Distinguish a runbook for a known alert from a playbook for an unknown failure.
Design verification and escalation points that stop a failed action from cascading.

entries.title: S3 Gateway Endpoints
entries.productionQuestion: A private subnet uploads to S3 and the NAT bill is large. What changes?
entries.learningDelta: A gateway endpoint adds a route to S3 in the route table, avoiding NAT data processing charges
objectives: Explain how a gateway endpoint routes S3 traffic through a prefix-list route instead of NAT.
Associate the right route tables and verify that S3 traffic actually left the NAT path.
Recognize a bucket policy that requires the endpoint and fails when traffic bypasses it.
Decide when a gateway endpoint is insufficient and an S3 interface endpoint is required.

entries.title: Savings Plans
entries.productionQuestion: You need flexibility across instance families. Do RIs or Savings Plans fit?
entries.learningDelta: Savings Plans commit to usage for a discount and are more flexible than RIs, but still require accurate forecasting
objectives: Explain what a Savings Plan commits to and what remains on-demand.
Compare Compute Savings Plans, EC2 Instance Savings Plans, and Reserved Instances.
Diagnose over-commitment and under-commitment from utilization and cost.
Choose a commitment level from forecast confidence rather than from the maximum discount.

entries.title: Scale to Zero
entries.productionQuestion: A dev environment is idle 80% of the time. Can it scale to zero?
entries.learningDelta: Scale-to-zero saves idle cost but adds cold-start latency and state loss; production-critical paths usually need a floor
objectives: Separate idle cost savings from the wake-up latency a scale-to-zero policy adds.
Explain why a floor of one task changes both the cost and the failure mode.
Diagnose the first-request timeout from idle policy, cold start, and client timeout.
Choose a scale-to-zero policy for a workload class and defend the tradeoff.

entries.title: Scaling Cooldowns and Stabilization
entries.productionQuestion: A one-minute spike triggers 30 tasks and then they all scale in. What do you change?
entries.learningDelta: Cooldowns and stabilization windows filter noise but delay response; the right values depend on workload duration
objectives: Explain how scale-out and scale-in cooldowns change a policy's response to bursty traffic.
Predict when a short burst will cause unnecessary capacity or a premature scale-in.
Choose cooldown values from burst duration, task startup time, and the cost of warm capacity.
Explain why a longer scale-in hold reduces churn but leaves idle tasks after the burst.

entries.title: Scheduled Scaling
entries.productionQuestion: Traffic doubles every weekday at 9 a.m. Why wait for reactive scaling?
entries.learningDelta: Scheduled scaling handles predictable demand; it must be combined with reactive policies for surprises
objectives: Map a known demand pattern to a scheduled capacity change.
Convert a UTC schedule into the local time the workload actually follows.
Diagnose a schedule that fires late or outside the traffic window.
Combine scheduled and reactive scaling without letting one erase the other.

entries.title: Scheduled Scaling Race Condition
entries.productionQuestion: A scheduled scale-down at 18:00 collides with an organic surge and capacity collapses. What do you change?
entries.learningDelta: Scheduled and dynamic scaling can race; minimum capacity, cooldowns, and change freezes prevent the overlap
objectives: Explain how a scheduled action and a dynamic policy both write the same desired capacity.
Diagnose the overlap from desired capacity, in-service capacity, demand, and error onset.
Choose a guardrail: minimum capacity, a frozen schedule, one capacity owner, or faster scale-out.
Defend the cost and recovery tradeoff of each guardrail.

entries.title: Schema Compatibility
entries.productionQuestion: Old and new versions run side by side for an hour. What schema rules apply?
entries.learningDelta: Rolling and canary releases require backward and forward compatible schemas; readers must tolerate missing and extra fields
objectives: Distinguish backward compatibility from forward compatibility during a rollout.
Explain why a required field breaks old readers while an additive field does not.
Sequence a schema change so old and new versions can coexist.
Test schema compatibility before and during a mixed-version window.

entries.title: Schema Registry and Compatibility
entries.productionQuestion: A producer adds a required field and old consumers crash. What compatibility mode?
entries.learningDelta: Schema compatibility modes govern evolution; backward, forward, and full compatibility have different deploy orders
objectives: Distinguish backward, forward, and full compatibility by who can read which data.
Predict which schema changes a compatibility mode will reject.
Choose a deploy order for producers and consumers from the compatibility direction.
Design an evolution that keeps old and new consumers working during rollout.

entries.title: Scrape Interval and Resolution
entries.productionQuestion: A 15-second scrape cannot show a 5-second spike. What do you change, and what does it cost?
entries.learningDelta: Sampling resolution bounds what you can detect; shorter intervals improve detection but increase ingest and cost
objectives: Relate scrape interval to the shortest outage the system can see.
Explain why a short spike can fall entirely between scrapes.
Quantify the ingest cost of a shorter interval.
Choose a resolution from the detection requirement and the budget.

entries.title: Seasonal Forecasting
entries.productionQuestion: Traffic grows 40% every December and the forecast is linear. What do you change?
entries.learningDelta: Forecasts need seasonality, growth, and uncertainty bands; capacity should be planned against a percentile, not a point estimate
objectives: Separate trend growth from seasonal uplift in a capacity forecast.
Explain why a confidence band on a linear forecast does not fix a missing seasonal term.
Diagnose an underprovisioned peak from utilization and shed load at the seasonal ramp.
Choose a planning percentile and defend its idle-capacity cost.

entries.title: Secrets in ECS
entries.productionQuestion: A database password is in an environment variable in the task definition. What is the safer path?
entries.learningDelta: Secrets Manager or SSM parameters can be injected at task start; image, task definition, and logs must stay free of secrets
objectives: Compare plaintext environment values with Secrets Manager and SSM Parameter Store references.
Trace when ECS resolves a secret and why a running task keeps the value it started with.
Choose a rotation path that does not depend on rebuilding the image or editing the task definition.
Design a least-privilege execution role for secret injection and a log policy that does not echo values.

entries.title: Secrets Management
entries.productionQuestion: A database password is rotated and 30 services fail. How do you rotate safely?
entries.learningDelta: Secrets Manager or SSM can store and rotate secrets, but consumers must refresh or restart; rotation is a distributed deploy
objectives: Trace a secret from rotation to every consumer and its connection pool.
Choose between runtime refresh and restart for a given consumer type.
Recognize stale credentials after rotation from authentication failures that look like a database outage.
Design a rotation that tolerates propagation delay and keeps a rollback path.

entries.title: Security Groups
entries.productionQuestion: A new service cannot be reached from the load balancer. Which security group rule?
entries.learningDelta: Security groups are stateful allow lists; references between groups are safer than CIDR ranges
objectives: Trace an ALB request through the load balancer security group and the target security group.
Explain why a target security group reference is narrower and easier to maintain than a CIDR range.
Use stateful return traffic and health-check behavior to separate a blocked rule from a missing route.
Replace a broad CIDR rule without breaking the service, and verify the target health signal.

entries.title: Service Discovery
entries.productionQuestion: A service calls another by IP and a task replacement breaks it. What do you use?
entries.learningDelta: Service discovery maps stable names to changing task IPs; DNS TTL and health determine failover
objectives: Explain how a stable DNS name resolves to changing task IPs.
Predict when a cached record can outlive the task it points to.
Choose a TTL and health-check strategy for a service that other services call.

entries.title: Severity Levels
entries.productionQuestion: One team calls an outage SEV1 and another calls the same thing SEV3. Why does it matter?
entries.learningDelta: Severity drives paging, communication, and authority; criteria must be based on user impact and scope, not on cause
objectives: Classify severity from user impact and scope rather than from the technical cause.
Explain how severity changes paging, communication cadence, and decision authority.
Recognize the cost of under-classification and the cost of over-classification.
Re-evaluate severity as scope becomes clearer during the incident.

entries.title: Severity Matrix
entries.productionQuestion: Two incidents with the same impact get different responses. What does the matrix need?
entries.learningDelta: A severity matrix maps user impact, scope, and duration to response levels; it must be simple enough to use under pressure
objectives: Map user impact, scope, and duration to a response level.
Keep the matrix small enough to classify without debate.
Test classification against realistic scenarios and disagreements.
Explain why exceptions and extra axes make responders fall back to gut feel.

entries.title: Shadow Traffic
entries.productionQuestion: You need production traffic to validate a rewrite but cannot affect users. What do you do?
entries.learningDelta: Shadow traffic mirrors requests to the new version and discards responses; it validates behavior but doubles load and risks side effects
objectives: Explain how request mirroring validates a new version without returning its responses.
Predict the load a shadow copy places on shared dependencies.
Identify write paths that must be suppressed or isolated before mirroring.
Design a shadow test that observes behavior without creating external effects.

entries.title: Shard Key Design
entries.productionQuestion: One shard key gives perfect distribution but every query is scatter-gather. What do you do?
entries.learningDelta: Shard keys must balance write distribution and query locality; high cardinality alone is not enough
objectives: Evaluate a shard key by cardinality, frequency, and whether it matches the dominant query shape.
Explain why a monotonically increasing ranged key concentrates new writes.
Predict when a hashed key distributes writes but turns range queries into scatter-gather.
Choose a compound or alternate key and state the cost of the choice.

entries.title: Sharding ALBs by Tenant or Hostname
entries.productionQuestion: One tenant's traffic saturates its ALB while other ALBs are idle. How do you shard?
entries.learningDelta: Sharding by hostname, path, or tenant reduces per-ALB connection pressure but requires routing consistency and per-shard observability
objectives: Choose a shard key that matches the tenant and session model.
Locate the hot shard instead of reading the fleet average.
Predict when a new shard will and will not reduce per-ALB load.
Preserve sessions while isolating a heavy tenant.

entries.title: Sharding Architecture
entries.productionQuestion: A sharded cluster routes queries slowly. Which component is involved?
entries.learningDelta: mongos routes queries using config server metadata; shards hold data, and routing decisions depend on the shard key
objectives: Place mongos, config servers, and shards on the query and metadata paths.
Explain why a query that omits the shard key fans out to every shard.
Distinguish routing and merge cost at mongos from storage work at a shard.
Recognize that config server metadata is cached by mongos and is not normally the per-query bottleneck.

entries.title: Sidecar Overhead
entries.productionQuestion: Latency rose after enabling the mesh. How much is the sidecar?
entries.learningDelta: Sidecars add hops, CPU, memory, and connection pools; the cost is visible in per-hop latency and resource usage
objectives: Separate mesh overhead from application latency on the same request path.
Compute sidecar CPU demand from per-pod request rate and hop count.
Explain how CPU throttling turns resource contention into tail latency.
Tune CPU limits and connection pools from measured per-hop cost.

entries.title: Sidecar Patterns
entries.productionQuestion: A sidecar doubles task CPU and the service is throttled. What do you check?
entries.learningDelta: Sidecars share task resources; CPU/memory limits and startup order affect the main container
objectives: Budget sidecar CPU and memory inside the task size rather than beside it.
Choose startup ordering and essential flags for proxy and log-router sidecars.
Distinguish main-container CPU throttling from sidecar startup failures.
Explain the blast radius of a sidecar that must stay alive with the application.

entries.title: Site-to-Site VPN
entries.productionQuestion: The VPN tunnel is up but traffic does not flow. What do you check?
entries.learningDelta: VPN requires matching tunnels, BGP or static routes, and security policies; tunnel state alone is not connectivity
objectives: Trace a site-to-site VPN packet through the tunnel, the route table, and the security policy.
Explain why a tunnel can be up while no route selects it, and why that differs from a policy block.
Compare static routing with BGP for failover between two tunnels.
Choose the smallest fix that restores traffic without hiding the next failure.

entries.title: SLI, SLO, SLA, and the Error Budget
entries.productionQuestion: Your SLO is 99.9% and the month is half over; how much failure can you still spend?
entries.learningDelta: An error budget converts an SLO into an allowed failure quantity; burn rate tells you when to stop shipping
objectives: Define an SLI as a ratio of good events to valid events.
Convert an SLO into an error budget for a compliance window.
Use burn rate to decide whether to keep shipping.
Explain why an SLA is not the same promise as an SLO.

entries.title: SLO Burn Rate: Alert on Speed, Not Just State
entries.productionQuestion: The 30-day SLO is still 99.9%, but the service has been failing for 40 minutes. Should you page?
entries.learningDelta: Multi-window burn-rate alerts catch fast burns early and slow burns reliably without paging on every blip
objectives: Compute burn rate from bad-event rate and the SLO allowance.
Explain why a short window confirms speed while a long window proves persistence.
Recognize a burn that a static error-rate alert cannot see.
Choose window lengths and a page threshold that fit the error budget.

entries.title: Slow Commands and the Redis Event Loop
entries.productionQuestion: Redis p99 spikes on every `KEYS *` call from a debug script. What is the mechanism?
entries.learningDelta: Redis executes commands on one thread per shard; O(N) commands and large values delay every other client
objectives: Explain how an O(N) command creates a latency spike that average CPU hides.
Read the slowlog, command statistics, and per-command latency to identify the blocking command.
Replace KEYS with a bounded SCAN loop and explain why total work does not disappear.
Choose a SCAN COUNT that bounds each call without multiplying command overhead.

entries.title: Slow Consumers
entries.productionQuestion: One consumer processes 10× slower than its peers. What do you check?
entries.learningDelta: Per-partition processing time, downstream calls, and poison records identify slow consumers; more consumers cannot split one partition
objectives: Find the slow consumer from per-partition lag and processing time instead of group averages.
Separate a slow downstream call from a hot key and from a poison record.
Explain why adding a consumer member cannot split one partition's work.
Choose a fix that preserves the ordering guarantee the consumer needs.

entries.title: Smoke Tests
entries.productionQuestion: A new task starts and serves 200 on `/health` but 500 on checkout. What smoke test?
entries.learningDelta: Smoke tests exercise real dependencies and critical writes; health checks alone prove only process liveness
objectives: Separate a liveness check from a smoke test that proves a user path works.
Design smoke tests that call real dependencies and read back writes.
Explain why a green smoke suite can still miss a broken checkout path.
Make smoke failure block promotion or trigger rollback.

entries.title: SNS and EventBridge Routing
entries.productionQuestion: A notification goes to five subscribers and a new event triggers three unintended consumers. What do you check?
entries.learningDelta: SNS fan-out and EventBridge rules solve different routing problems; broad patterns and shared buses create hidden consumers and ordering surprises
objectives: Distinguish SNS topic fan-out from EventBridge rule matching.
Predict delivery volume from subscriptions, rules, and event rate.
Diagnose hidden consumers caused by a broad event pattern.
Design routing that bounds fan-out and keeps unrelated teams decoupled.

entries.title: SOC 2 for Engineers
entries.productionQuestion: An enterprise customer asks for SOC 2. Which controls need evidence?
entries.learningDelta: SOC 2 reports on security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy; evidence must come from operating controls
objectives: Map the five SOC 2 trust services criteria to concrete engineering controls.
Distinguish a control that exists in policy from one that produced operating evidence during the period.
Design evidence capture that is continuous, attributable, and fresh enough to sample.
Explain what an exception in a SOC 2 report does and does not mean.

entries.title: Split Brain: Two Writers, One Truth
entries.productionQuestion: Two database nodes both accept writes during a network partition. How do you recover?
entries.learningDelta: Split brain requires fencing, quorum, or a single-writer design; reconciliation after divergence is expensive and sometimes impossible
objectives: Explain why a network partition lets both database nodes believe they are the writer.
Compare quorum, a witness, and fencing, and name the failure each control does not cover.
Estimate divergent writes from the dual-writer window and the write rate.
Choose a recovery path when both sides already contain accepted writes.

entries.title: Spot Interruptions
entries.productionQuestion: Spot instances are 70% cheaper but tasks disappear. Which workloads fit?
entries.learningDelta: Spot capacity is interruptible with notice; stateless, checkpointed, and drainable workloads tolerate it
objectives: Decide which workloads can run on interruptible capacity.
Design a checkpoint and drain path that limits lost work.
Diagnose a fleet that loses capacity without a fallback.
Balance Spot share against completion and cost risk.

entries.title: SQS FIFO
entries.productionQuestion: You need per-customer order and high throughput. How does FIFO scale?
entries.learningDelta: FIFO queues preserve order within a message group; throughput scales with groups, and a hot group serializes
objectives: Explain how a FIFO queue orders messages within a message group.
Predict throughput when consumers outnumber message groups.
Diagnose a hot group that serializes despite a large consumer fleet.
Redesign a group key to spread load without breaking per-customer order.

entries.title: SQS Visibility Timeout
entries.productionQuestion: A consumer takes longer than the visibility timeout and the message is processed twice. What do you change?
entries.learningDelta: Visibility timeout hides a message while it is processed; it must exceed processing time or be extended, and failures need a DLQ
objectives: Explain what the visibility timeout hides and when the message becomes visible again.
Predict duplicate deliveries when processing time exceeds visibility.
Choose between a longer timeout, heartbeat extension, and a DLQ.
Design a retry path that does not turn slow processing into repeated side effects.

entries.title: Status Pages
entries.productionQuestion: Users report failures before the status page updates. What should it say?
entries.learningDelta: Status pages communicate known impact and next update time; they must not speculate on cause or blame a provider prematurely
objectives: Publish a first status update from known impact without waiting for a root cause.
State a next update time and hold it even when nothing has changed.
Keep speculation and premature blame out of the public page.
Measure the support and trust cost of an outdated status page.

entries.title: Step Scaling
entries.productionQuestion: Traffic crosses a threshold repeatedly and the service flaps between 4 and 20 tasks. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Step scaling uses thresholds and cooldowns; missing scale-in stabilization causes oscillation and cold starts
objectives: Explain how a step scaling policy turns CloudWatch alarm breaches into task count changes.
Predict how threshold placement and scale-in stabilization interact with a repeating traffic wave.
Distinguish a capacity shortfall from a policy that is oscillating between scale-out and scale-in.
Design a step policy that holds enough ready capacity through the wave without flapping.

entries.title: Sticky Sessions: Affinity and Its Cost
entries.productionQuestion: A session-heavy app loses carts when targets scale in. What is the tradeoff of stickiness?
entries.learningDelta: Sticky sessions preserve affinity but reduce load balance, complicate draining, and can concentrate load on a few targets
objectives: Explain how an ALB cookie binds a session to a target.
Predict when stickiness concentrates load on one target.
Trace what happens to a sticky session when a target drains or fails.
Choose between target affinity and a shared session store.

entries.title: Storage Autoscaling
entries.productionQuestion: Disk usage climbs and autoscaling has a maximum. What happens at the cap?
entries.learningDelta: Storage autoscaling adds capacity within a maximum; growth rate, retention, and temporary files determine whether it saves you
objectives: Compute time to full from free space and growth rate.
Explain autoscaling increments and the maximum storage cap.
Separate permanent data growth from temporary files and retention.
Choose a cap and an alarm that leave recovery headroom.

entries.title: Storage Lifecycle
entries.productionQuestion: Storage cost grows every month and most objects are never read. What do you do?
entries.learningDelta: Lifecycle policies transition and expire data; retrieval cost and latency must match access patterns
objectives: Map object age and access pattern to a lifecycle transition.
Explain how an early transition turns a hot read into an expensive retrieval.
Diagnose an expiry rule that deletes data the workload still reads.
Choose a transition point that balances storage savings against retrieval risk.

entries.title: Structured Logging: Fields Over Sentences
entries.productionQuestion: You need every log line for one request across 20 tasks. What must the log schema contain?
entries.learningDelta: Structured fields, request IDs, and stable event names make logs searchable; prose logs do not
objectives: Identify the fields that let one request be reconstructed across tasks.
Explain why JSON formatting without a correlation identifier is still unsearchable.
Read query success, search latency, and volume as separate log-pipeline signals.
Design a log event schema that survives service boundaries and deploys.

entries.title: Subnets and Route Tables
entries.productionQuestion: A new subnet has instances but no internet access. Which route is missing?
entries.learningDelta: A subnet is associated with one route table; the longest prefix match and target determine where traffic goes
objectives: Explain how a subnet's route table association decides which routes the subnet can use.
Read a route table by destination, target, and state instead of by route count.
Predict which route wins when a more specific prefix shadows a default route.
Distinguish a missing association, a missing default route, and a blackhole target.

entries.title: Subprocessor Management
entries.productionQuestion: A vendor adds a subprocessor in another region and your residency promise breaks. How do you prevent it?
entries.learningDelta: Subprocessor obligations require notice, approval, flow-down terms, and a maintained inventory
objectives: Explain how a subprocessor differs from the direct vendor and why the chain changes the risk.
Design notice and approval gates that treat a new subprocessor as a material change.
Check whether equivalent security, breach, deletion, and residency terms actually flow down.
Keep an inventory that can answer where regulated data is processed at any time.

entries.title: Symptom-Based Alerting
entries.productionQuestion: The CPU alert pages every night at 2 a.m. and users are fine. What should page instead?
entries.learningDelta: Symptom alerts track SLO impact; cause alerts support diagnosis but create noise and do not prove user impact
objectives: Classify an alert as a symptom or a cause using the signal it measures.
Compare page volume with user impact for each alert type.
Explain why a high-CPU page with healthy latency and errors is a ticket, not a page.
Redesign a paging policy around SLO impact while keeping cause signals for diagnosis.

entries.title: Synthetic Monitoring: Probe the Path
entries.productionQuestion: Users in one region cannot reach the app while your servers are healthy. What probes reveal it?
entries.learningDelta: Synthetic probes exercise the real path from multiple locations; interval and location coverage determine detection time
objectives: Read a synthetic check as a path from a location through DNS, TLS, and HTTP.
Separate a green probe from proof that every user path is healthy.
Compute detection time from interval and confirmation count.
Choose probe coverage that finds a regional edge failure before users report it.

entries.title: Tail Sampling: Keep the Interesting Traces
entries.productionQuestion: Storage budget allows 2% of traces, but you need every timeout. How do you sample?
entries.learningDelta: Tail sampling buffers completed traces and applies policies, preserving errors and latency outliers at bounded volume
objectives: Size a tail-sampling buffer from arrival rate, decision wait, and collector count.
Explain why a dropped trace never reaches a policy, even an error policy.
Compare error, latency, and baseline policies by what they retain and cost.
Recognize when the decision wait must grow to cover long traces.

entries.title: Target Tracking Scaling
entries.productionQuestion: CPU stays at 40% while latency rises and the service does not scale. What metric should drive scaling?
entries.learningDelta: Target tracking follows a metric and a target; choosing CPU when the bottleneck is queue depth or concurrency causes late scaling
objectives: Explain how a target tracking policy turns a metric and a target into a task count.
Choose a scaling metric that moves with the real bottleneck.
Predict when a policy will not scale because its metric stays below target.
Tune the target and cooldown without creating oscillation or sustained shortfall.

entries.title: Task Draining
entries.productionQuestion: A deployment causes 502s during task stop. What is the drain sequence?
entries.learningDelta: ECS deregisters a task, waits for draining, then stops it; timeout and connection behavior decide in-flight request loss
objectives: Order the deregistration, drain, SIGTERM, and stop steps for an ECS task.
Choose a deregistration delay and stop timeout from request duration and connection behavior.
Explain why a short drain window produces 502s during an otherwise healthy deployment.

entries.title: Task IAM Roles
entries.productionQuestion: A task needs S3 access but the node role can read everything. What do you change?
entries.learningDelta: Task roles are per-task credentials delivered by the agent; execution roles are separate and used to pull images and write logs
objectives: Separate the task role from the execution role and name what each one authorizes.
Trace how an ECS task receives temporary credentials without static access keys.
Scope a task policy to the workload's real access need without breaking image pulls or logs.

entries.title: Telemetry Cost Governance
entries.productionQuestion: Telemetry cost grows faster than traffic and no one owns it. What is the governance model?
entries.learningDelta: Cost governance uses budgets, cardinality limits, sampling, retention tiers, and ownership; observability is a product with a unit cost
objectives: Build a unit-cost model for metrics, logs, and traces.
Separate cost growth caused by traffic from growth caused by cardinality and retention.
Defend a telemetry cut by naming the coverage it preserves and the coverage it loses.
Assign ownership and a review cadence for a telemetry budget.

entries.title: The Balancer
entries.productionQuestion: Chunks are imbalanced but the balancer is off. Should you turn it on during peak?
entries.learningDelta: The balancer improves distribution over time but adds load; windows and thresholds determine whether it helps during an incident
objectives: Explain when the balancer starts migrating and when it leaves a cluster alone.
Distinguish a cluster that is imbalanced from one that is actively migrating.
Predict how balancing during peak traffic changes latency before it improves distribution.
Choose between an immediate rebalance and a scheduled balancing window.

entries.title: The Cost of Headroom
entries.productionQuestion: Finance asks why 40% of capacity is idle. How do you justify it?
entries.learningDelta: Headroom is insurance against failure and peaks; the right level depends on SLO, failure domain size, and traffic variability
objectives: Quantify the monthly cost of headroom above peak demand.
Size N+1 from the largest failure domain and the post-failure SLO target.
Distinguish exact N+1 from headroom that absorbs variability and failover.
Defend a headroom level with a cost and risk comparison.

entries.title: The Queueing Knee: Why 70% Is the New 100%
entries.productionQuestion: CPU is at 75% and p99 doubled; is the system healthy?
entries.learningDelta: Queueing latency is nonlinear; near saturation, small load increases create large latency increases
objectives: Explain why queueing delay grows faster than utilization near the knee.
Predict when a small load increase will breach a latency SLO.
Separate utilization headroom from variability headroom.
Choose a mitigation that addresses load, service time, or arrival burstiness.

entries.title: Timeouts: Budgets That Travel With the Request
entries.productionQuestion: A request has 800ms total and three calls; which timeout do you set?
entries.learningDelta: Timeouts must be smaller than the caller's remaining budget and must propagate a deadline, not restart it
objectives: Derive per-hop timeouts from an end-to-end request budget.
Explain why a deadline is not the same as a fresh timeout at each hop.
Recognize pool saturation caused by work that outlives the caller.
Choose between a tighter timeout, a shorter chain, and load shedding.

entries.title: TLS Handshakes: Latency Before the Request
entries.productionQuestion: p99 rose after a DNS change; is TLS or the application slow?
entries.learningDelta: Full handshakes add round trips and CPU; resumption and keep-alive remove them from the steady state
objectives: Trace where TCP and TLS handshake time sits relative to application time.
Calculate how keep-alive and session resumption change handshake frequency.
Separate handshake CPU cost from request queuing using per-phase signals.
Reduce handshake cost without weakening certificate or protocol validation.

entries.title: TLS Termination: Where Keys Live
entries.productionQuestion: You need end-to-end encryption but the ALB must route by path. Where do you terminate?
entries.learningDelta: TLS can terminate at edge, load balancer, or service; each choice changes certificate scope, inspection, and latency
objectives: Trace where TLS ends and where private keys live at each termination layer.
Explain why path routing and Layer 7 inspection require a terminator that sees HTTP.
Choose re-encryption or mTLS to keep traffic protected past the load balancer.
Compare edge, load balancer, and service termination by certificate scope and operational cost.

entries.title: Toil Reduction
entries.productionQuestion: The team spends 40% of on-call on the same manual cleanup. How do you reduce it?
entries.learningDelta: Toil is repetitive, manual, and scalable work; measure it, automate the top tasks, and protect the time
objectives: Distinguish toil from necessary operational work and project work.
Measure toil by task, frequency, time, and error risk.
Automate the highest-value manual task before adding prevention work.
Protect engineering capacity so cleanup does not consume prevention.

entries.title: Traffic Shifting
entries.productionQuestion: You need 1%, 5%, 25%, 100% with a gate at each step. How do you sequence it?
entries.learningDelta: Traffic shifting is a sequence of exposure steps with gates; step size trades detection time for blast radius
objectives: Sequence a rollout through exposure steps with a gate after each step.
Calculate the blast radius of a step from traffic share and defect rate.
Explain why a larger step improves sample size but exposes more users before a gate can act.
Choose a step size and gate window that keep exposure inside an agreed budget.

entries.title: Traffic Splitting
entries.productionQuestion: You need 5% canary traffic and instant rollback. Where do you implement it?
entries.learningDelta: Mesh traffic splitting weights clusters by route; it is fast to change but must align with observability and health
objectives: Place a weighted split at the proxy route instead of changing clients.
Calculate the observed error rate when one version has a higher failure share.
Explain why a weight change can expose an unready version.
Design a rollback that restores the stable version without a deploy.

entries.title: Transactional Outbox
entries.productionQuestion: The database commit succeeds and the Kafka publish fails. How do you keep them consistent?
entries.learningDelta: The outbox pattern writes the event in the same transaction and publishes it asynchronously, using polling or CDC
objectives: Explain why a database commit and a broker publish cannot be one atomic operation.
Predict lost or phantom events from a dual write under publish failure.
Compare polling and change data capture for draining an outbox.
Design an at-least-once publisher and an idempotent consumer.

entries.title: Transactions and Their Limits
entries.productionQuestion: A transaction spans 10 minutes and 50k documents. What breaks first?
entries.learningDelta: MongoDB transactions have time and size limits and hold resources; they are not a substitute for schema design
objectives: Explain what a multi-document transaction holds while it runs: a snapshot, locks, and cache.
Identify the default lifetime limit and the cache error that aborts an oversized transaction.
Separate a transaction boundary problem from a schema or query problem.
Design a retry and abort path that keeps a failed transaction from becoming a retry loop.

entries.title: TTL Jitter and Smearing
entries.productionQuestion: A batch warmup gives every key the same TTL and the cache expires in waves. What do you change?
entries.learningDelta: TTL jitter spreads expiration, smoothing backend load and reducing synchronized refreshes
objectives: Recognize an expiry wave from its period and its alignment with a batch load.
Add jitter at the point where the TTL is written, including warmups and deploys.
Quantify how jitter lowers the peak while leaving total refresh work unchanged.
Bound the extra staleness that a longer maximum TTL introduces.

entries.title: Unit Economics
entries.productionQuestion: A feature is profitable at 1k users and loses money at 1M. Which cost dominates?
entries.learningDelta: Unit economics combine compute, storage, network, and observability per unit of value; fixed costs hide until scale
objectives: Separate contribution margin per user from total monthly profit.
Diagnose why a feature that works at small scale fails at large scale.
Price a feature from its variable cost and its fixed-cost recovery point.
Choose the operating metric that catches margin erosion before the bill does.

entries.title: Upstream Connection Reuse
entries.productionQuestion: Backends see a connection storm after every deploy even though traffic is flat. Why?
entries.learningDelta: Connection pools and keep-alive must be warmed and drained alongside targets; new targets without reuse multiply handshakes
objectives: Separate steady-state connection churn from deploy-driven connection churn.
Explain why a new target starts with a cold upstream pool.
Measure the connection and latency cost of a rolling deploy.
Design pool warmup and draining that do not create a new storm.

entries.title: USE and RED: Two Lenses on One System
entries.productionQuestion: Is this a resource problem or a request-path problem, and which signal set tells you first?
entries.learningDelta: USE finds saturated resources; RED finds sick request paths; using one where the other belongs hides the cause
objectives: Tell a resource problem from a request-path problem before choosing a dashboard.
Read utilization, saturation, and errors as three separate resource signals.
Read rate, errors, and duration as three separate service signals.
Explain how a buffered write path keeps RED green while the disk saturates.

entries.title: Vacuum and Bloat
entries.productionQuestion: A table grows despite deletes and queries slow down. What is bloat doing?
entries.learningDelta: PostgreSQL MVCC keeps dead tuples until vacuum; bloat increases I/O and can make plans worse, while aggressive vacuum competes for resources
objectives: Explain why DELETE and UPDATE leave dead tuples instead of reclaiming space immediately.
Relate dead-tuple accumulation to update rate, vacuum frequency, and the oldest snapshot.
Distinguish reusable space from disk that is returned to the operating system.
Choose between tuning autovacuum, scheduling maintenance, and rewriting a table.

entries.title: Vendor Risk
entries.productionQuestion: A critical vendor has no security review and an outage exposes customer data. What did you miss?
entries.learningDelta: Vendor risk covers security, availability, data handling, subcontractors, and exit; criticality determines depth
objectives: Assign vendor criticality from data access, availability dependency, and substitutability.
Match assessment depth and evidence to each tier instead of applying one questionnaire to every vendor.
Evaluate subcontractor visibility and a tested exit path as part of the same risk decision.
Prioritize a vendor portfolio before an incident forces the review.

entries.title: VictoriaMetrics and High Cardinality
entries.productionQuestion: A label with request IDs makes the series count explode. What happens to memory and query time?
entries.learningDelta: Series cardinality drives index and memory cost; high-cardinality labels belong in logs or traces, not metric labels
objectives: Estimate active series from metric names, hosts, and label values.
Explain how a high-cardinality label raises index memory and query time.
Distinguish series cardinality from sample volume and retention.
Move an identifier-level question out of metrics without losing the answer.

entries.title: VictoriaMetrics Architecture: Ingest, Store, Query
entries.productionQuestion: Metrics arrive late and queries time out during a rollout. Which VictoriaMetrics component is the bottleneck?
entries.learningDelta: vminsert, vmstorage, and vmselect have separate scaling limits; ingestion, storage, and query pressure must be diagnosed separately
objectives: Map a VictoriaMetrics cluster symptom to vminsert, vmstorage, or vmselect.
Separate ingestion pressure from query pressure using component-level signals.
Explain why adding storage nodes does not fix a query fan-out bottleneck.
Choose the component to scale and state the tradeoff of that choice.

entries.title: VPC Endpoints
entries.productionQuestion: S3 traffic is expensive through NAT. How do you keep it private?
entries.learningDelta: Gateway endpoints keep S3/DynamoDB traffic on the AWS network; interface endpoints use ENIs and security groups
objectives: Choose a gateway or interface endpoint from the service, source network, and access-control requirements.
Trace whether AWS service traffic uses the endpoint or the NAT gateway.
Explain why an endpoint policy denial does not fall back to NAT.
Use route association, private DNS, endpoint policy, and security groups in the right order.

entries.title: VPC Flow Logs
entries.productionQuestion: The app sees no request and the client sees a timeout. Did the packet reach the instance?
entries.learningDelta: Flow logs record accepted and rejected flows at the ENI; they show direction, action, and bytes, but not payload
objectives: Read a flow log record as a five-tuple plus action, direction, and bytes.
Use ACCEPT and REJECT records to localize a drop to the security group or network ACL.
Explain what a missing record does and does not prove.
Choose the log point and fields that answer a specific packet question.

entries.title: VPC Fundamentals
entries.productionQuestion: Two services cannot reach each other and both have public IPs. What is the first network boundary?
entries.learningDelta: A VPC is an isolated network with its own address space, route tables, and gateways; public IPs do not imply reachability
objectives: Explain what a VPC boundary is and why a public IP is an address rather than a path.
Trace a private packet through the source route table, the peering attachment, and the peer route table.
Distinguish a missing route from a blackhole route and from a missing return path.
Decide when to restore a peering connection, add routes, or choose a different connectivity service.

entries.title: VPC Peering vs Transit Gateway
entries.productionQuestion: Ten VPCs need full connectivity. Do you mesh peering or use a transit gateway?
entries.learningDelta: Peering is pairwise and non-transitive; Transit Gateway is a hub with attachments, route tables, and centralized policy
objectives: Calculate the number of peering connections a full mesh needs and explain why the count grows quadratically.
Show why a chain of peering connections does not give every VPC a path to every other VPC.
Compare peering and Transit Gateway on attachment model, route ownership, and segmentation.
Choose a topology from VPC count, operational ownership, and the need for centralized routing.

entries.title: WAF and Edge Rate Limits
entries.productionQuestion: A credential-stuffing wave is exhausting the login service. Where do you enforce limits?
entries.learningDelta: Edge WAF rules and rate limits stop abuse before compute, but thresholds and match conditions decide false positives
objectives: Place a rate-based WAF rule where it protects the login service without counting unrelated traffic.
Measure attack pass-through and legitimate-user false positives together.
Explain why a per-IP threshold can miss a distributed attack and block a shared NAT.
Tune a rule in count mode before enforcing it at the edge.

entries.title: WAF and Shield Together
entries.productionQuestion: A Layer 7 attack passes the WAF and saturates the origin. What layer failed?
entries.learningDelta: Shield protects volumetric L3/L4; WAF inspects L7 requests; neither replaces origin capacity or rate limiting
objectives: Separate a volumetric L3/L4 attack from an application-layer L7 request flood.
Read origin utilization and error rate when the WAF is blocking most requests.
Explain why a high block percentage can still leave the origin saturated.
Layer Shield, WAF rules, rate limiting, and origin capacity without treating one as a complete defense.

entries.title: Warm Pools
entries.productionQuestion: Autoscaling takes 3 minutes to add capacity. Do you keep warm instances?
entries.learningDelta: Warm pools trade idle cost for faster scale-out; pool size must match the ramp rate, not the peak
objectives: Explain how a warm pool shortens time-to-capacity during a ramp.
Size a pool from the ramp gap rather than from peak demand.
Diagnose a pool that is exhausted before the traffic peak arrives.
Quantify the idle capacity a pool holds when demand is flat.

entries.title: WarpStream on Object Storage
entries.productionQuestion: A Kafka-compatible service stores data in object storage. What changes for latency and cost?
entries.learningDelta: Object-storage streaming trades broker-local disk for S3 latency and cost; tail latency and metadata operations dominate
objectives: Explain how a Kafka-compatible service can keep data in object storage instead of broker disks.
Relate batch interval and partition count to object request rate, latency, and cost.
Distinguish throughput capacity from tail latency in an object-storage streaming design.
Choose when the architecture fits and when broker-local storage is still required.

entries.title: WebSockets Through a Load Balancer
entries.productionQuestion: WebSocket clients disconnect every 60 seconds behind the ALB. What setting is involved?
entries.learningDelta: WebSockets reuse a long-lived TCP connection; idle timeouts, draining, and connection limits behave differently from short HTTP requests
objectives: Explain the HTTP Upgrade handshake and what changes after a 101 response.
Find an idle timeout that closes an apparently active WebSocket.
Predict how deregistration delay turns a deploy into a reconnect wave.
Design heartbeat, draining, and reconnect behavior for a WebSocket fleet.

entries.title: Write Amplification
entries.productionQuestion: Write throughput drops and disk I/O is saturated. What is write amplification doing?
entries.learningDelta: Indexes, journaling, replication, and document growth multiply physical writes; more indexes can hurt write capacity
objectives: Break one logical write into its document, index, journal, and replication work.
Predict how index count and document growth change physical I/O per write.
Separate a disk-capacity problem from a CPU or network problem using write-path signals.
Reduce write amplification without silently dropping the indexes reads depend on.

entries.title: Write Concern
entries.productionQuestion: A write is acknowledged and then lost after a primary crash. What write concern was used?
entries.learningDelta: Write concern controls how many nodes acknowledge before success; w:1 is fast but can lose writes on failover
objectives: Explain what `w:1`, `w:2`, and `w:"majority"` wait for before returning success.
Distinguish journal durability on one node from replication to a majority.
Predict which acknowledged writes can be lost when the primary is replaced.
Choose a write concern from the product's durability and latency requirements.

entries.title: Write-Behind: Speed With a Data-Loss Window
entries.productionQuestion: Write-behind makes writes 10× faster, but the cache crashes. What is lost?
entries.learningDelta: Write-behind acknowledges before durable storage, creating a loss window and ordering complexity
objectives: Quantify the loss window from write rate and flush delay.
Explain why cache persistence does not automatically make an acknowledged write durable.
Identify ordering and read-your-writes hazards in concurrent flushes.
Decide which data classes can accept asynchronous durability and which cannot.

entries.title: Zero Trust
entries.productionQuestion: A compromised internal host can reach every service. What changes?
entries.learningDelta: Zero trust authenticates and authorizes each service request; network location is not identity
objectives: Explain why an internal IP address or security group is not an authorization decision.
Separate workload authentication from per-request authorization.
Recognize a flat network's blast radius when one internal host is compromised.
Design a zero-trust rollout that adds identity checks without blocking legitimate service calls.

entries.title: Zonal Isolation: Survive an AZ Loss
entries.productionQuestion: One AZ is impaired and the service degrades more than expected. What shared dependency crossed zones?
entries.learningDelta: Zonal isolation requires independent targets, load balancer nodes, NAT, and dependencies per zone
objectives: Size each zone for the loss of another zone, not for its even share.
Find dependencies that cross the zone boundary and correlate failures.
Explain what cross-zone load balancing does and does not fix.
Design a failover test that exercises the real dependency graph.
